The perimeter is the total length around the triangle: add the three sides.
The equilateral triangle has the same perimeter, 21 cm, and its 3 sides are all equal, so divide by 3.
Check: three sides of 7 cm give the same perimeter.

questions.stem: There are 60 pupils in a school. 6 of these pupils wear glasses. Exactly half of the 60 pupils in the school are boys. From this information, what percentage of boys in this school wear glasses?
questions.hint: To find a percentage of the boys, you need to know HOW MANY BOYS wear glasses. Check whether the information tells you that, or try two different possibilities.

keyPoints.note: The 6 pupils could be boys, girls or a mixture. The question does not say which.
You need (boys who wear glasses) ÷ (all boys) × 100, and the first number is unknown.

steps.explain: Half of the 60 pupils are boys, so we know the number of boys.
The percentage of boys who wear glasses is the number of boys with glasses divided by 30. But the question only tells us that 6 pupils (boys or girls) wear glasses.

questions.stem: On a farm 80 sheep gave birth. 30% of the sheep gave birth to two lambs each. The rest of the sheep gave birth to just one lamb each. How many sheep are there altogether?
questions.hint: Lambs are sheep too! Find how many lambs were born, then add them to the 80 sheep (the mothers) that were already on the farm.

keyPoints.note: 30% of 80 sheep had twins; the other 70% had one lamb each.
Altogether includes the 80 mother sheep AND all the new lambs.

steps.explain: Find how many sheep had two lambs: 30% of 80.
The rest had one lamb each: subtract from 80.
Count the lambs born. 24 sheep had 2 lambs each and 56 sheep had 1 lamb each.
Total number of lambs.
The question asks for the number of sheep altogether, which includes the 80 mothers and the 104 lambs.
Common mistake: 104 counts the lambs only, and 48 or 56 count only some of them. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A team has \(\$90.00\) to buy balls. One ball costs \(\$7\). The team gets every fifth ball for free. What is the largest number of balls the team can get?
questions.hint: Think in groups of 5 balls: you pay for 4 balls and get the 5th free. Find the cost of one group, then see how many whole groups the money buys and whether the leftover can buy anything.

keyPoints.note: In each group of 5 balls you pay for only 4 balls.
After buying whole groups, check if the leftover money can still buy one more ball.

steps.explain: In each group of 5 balls the 5th is free, so the team pays for 4 balls only.
See how many groups of 5 balls the team can afford with \(\$90\).
3 groups cost \(\$84\) and give \(3\times5=15\) balls. The team has \(\$6\) left.
One more ball costs \(\$7\), but only \(\$6\) is left, so no more balls can be bought. (Buying a 4th group would need \(\$112\).)
So the largest number of balls is 15. Check: the 15 balls cost 12 paid balls: \(12\times\$7=\$84\le\$90\). \(\checkmark\) The 16th ball would need \(\$84+\$7=\$91\gt\$90\).

questions.stem:
At a grocery store, jobs are recorded on a Venn diagram like the one below.

If an employee only works as a checker and in the deli, in which region of the diagram does the employee belong?

questions.hint: Each circle is one job. A region inside two circles means the employee does both jobs. The word “only” means the employee must NOT be inside the third circle.

keyPoints.text: only works as a checker and in the deli
keyPoints.note: Inside the Checker circle AND the Deli circle, but outside the Stocker circle.
Check the four labelled regions W, X, Y, Z one by one.

questions.stem: Jane and Kate are ski racing. They both start at the same place, at the same time, and follow the same path. Jane is travelling at 5m/s and Kate is traveling at 8m/s. How many metres ahead is Kate after one minute?
questions.hint: The speeds are in metres per SECOND but the time is one MINUTE. Convert the time to seconds first, then find how far each skier travels using distance \(=\) speed \(\times\) time.

keyPoints.note: m/s means metres per SECOND.
One minute is 60 seconds, so change the time to seconds before multiplying.

steps.explain: The speeds are in metres per second, so change one minute into seconds.
Distance \(=\) speed \(\times\) time. Find how far Jane travels.
Find how far Kate travels.
Kate is ahead by the difference between the two distances.
Check with a shortcut: Kate gains \(8-5=3\) metres every second, so in 60 seconds she gains \(3\times60\) metres.

questions.stem: I multiply three positive integers that are greater than 1 and get 333. Find the one of the numbers.
questions.hint: Break 333 into prime factors. Three numbers greater than 1 whose product is 333 must use up all of its prime factors.

keyPoints.note: None of the three integers can be 1, so each one must contain at least one prime factor of 333.
Start by writing 333 as a product of prime numbers.

steps.explain: Test divisibility by 3: the digits of 333 add to \(3+3+3=9\), which is a multiple of 3, so 333 is divisible by 3.
The number 111 also has digit sum 3, so it is divisible by 3 again.
37 is a prime number (not divisible by 2, 3, 5 and \(7\times7\gt37\)). So the prime factorisation of 333 is:
333 has exactly three prime factors, so three integers greater than 1 must be one prime factor each: the numbers are 3, 3 and 37. The only option that is one of these numbers is 3.
Check the other options. 9: \(9\times37=333\) uses only two numbers (the third would have to be 1). 111: \(111\times3=333\) again leaves 1. 11 does not divide 333 at all.

questions.stem: What is 54321 less than the product of 30001 and 54321?
questions.hint: “Less than” means subtract from the product. Notice that 54321 appears twice, so you can avoid a long multiplication by factorising.

keyPoints.note: “54321 less than X” means X − 54321. The order matters.
Product means multiply: 30001 × 54321.

steps.explain: Translate into numbers. “Less than” means subtract 54321 from the product.
Both terms contain 54321, so take it out as a common factor: \(a\times b-b=(a-1)\times b\).
Simplify the bracket.
Multiply 54321 by 3, then add four zeros (because \(30000=3\times10\,000\)).
Put the zeros on the end.
Check the size: \(30\,000\times54\,000\approx1.6\) billion, so the answer has 10 digits and starts with 1.6. This matches 1,629,630,000 and rules out the other options.

questions.stem: At a stationery shop, a pack of five notebooks costs \(\$5\) and a pack of nine notebooks costs \(\$8\). What is the least amount of money do I need to buy 77 notebooks?
questions.hint: Compare the price of ONE notebook in each pack to see which pack is the better buy. Then buy as many of the better pack as possible, making sure the total is exactly 77 notebooks.

keyPoints.note: Use the cheaper pack (cost per notebook) as much as possible.
You need at least 77 notebooks, and the packs must add to exactly 77 to avoid wasting money.

steps.explain: Find the cost of one notebook in each pack. The 5-pack costs \(\$5\div5\) per notebook and the 9-pack costs \(\$8\div9\).
The 9-pack is cheaper per notebook, so buy as many 9-packs as possible. See how many fit into 77.
8 packs of nine give 72 notebooks, leaving exactly 5 more notebooks to buy: that is one 5-pack.
Work out the cost.

Check other ways. Using 3 nine-packs and 10 five-packs also makes 77 (\(27+50\)), but costs \(24+50=\$74\). Buying 9 nine-packs gives 81 notebooks and costs \(\$72\), which is more. So \(\$69\) is the least.

questions.stem: There are 15 men on a basketball team, and in a game 5 of them play at any one time. If the game is 48 minutes long and if each man plays exactly the same amount of time, how many minutes does each man play?
questions.hint: Count the total “player-minutes” on court during the game (5 players for 48 minutes), then share that total equally between all 15 men.

keyPoints.text: 5 of them play at any one time
keyPoints.note: At every moment 5 players are on court, so the total playing time is 5 × 48 minutes.

keyPoints.text: exactly the same amount of time
keyPoints.note: Share the total equally among all 15 men.

steps.explain: At any moment 5 players are on court. Over a 48-minute game, the total playing time of all players added together is:
This 240 minutes of playing time is shared equally among the 15 men.
Divide: 15 goes into 240 sixteen times (\(15\times16=240\)).
Check with a fraction: each man plays \(\dfrac{5}{15}=\dfrac13\) of the game, and one third of 48 minutes is 16 minutes. \(\checkmark\)

questions.hint: They all walk at the same speed, so whoever walks the greatest distance finishes last. Count the number of block-lengths along each coloured route: go along a path one straight piece at a time and add up.

keyPoints.note: Same speed means the LONGEST route takes the longest time. You only need to compare route lengths.
The child with the greatest number of blocks to walk finishes last.

steps.explain: All four walk at the same speed, so the child who walks the longest distance arrives last. We count the length of each route in block-lengths (one side of a square block).

questions.stem: A right-angled isosceles triangle must have
options: two right angles and two equal sides
two equal sides and one right angle
one right angle and different sides
questions.hint: Split the name into two clues: “right-angled” tells you about an angle, “isosceles” tells you about sides. Remember the three angles of any triangle add up to 180°.

keyPoints.note: Right-angled = exactly one 90° angle. Isosceles = two equal sides.

steps.explain: The name has two parts. “Right-angled” means the triangle has a right angle (\(90^\circ\)). “Isosceles” means it has two equal sides.

steps.explain: Can a triangle have two right angles? The three angles of a triangle add to \(180^\circ\), and two right angles already use \(90^\circ+90^\circ=180^\circ\), leaving \(0^\circ\) for the third angle, which is impossible.
So options A and B (two or three right angles) are impossible. A triangle can have only ONE right angle.
Option D says the sides are all different. But isosceles means two sides are equal, so D contradicts the name.
Option C matches both clues: two equal sides and one right angle. Check: the two equal sides are the legs next to the right angle, and the other two angles are each \((180^\circ-90^\circ)\div2\).

questions.stem: 7 identical pipes fill 3 identical tanks in 45 minutes. 5 of the same pipes will fill one of these tanks in
questions.hint: Find the time for 7 pipes to fill ONE tank, then the time for ONE pipe to fill one tank. Fewer pipes take longer, so multiply when you go down to 1 pipe and divide when you go up to 5 pipes.

keyPoints.note: First reduce to ONE tank: 3 tanks take 45 minutes, so 1 tank takes a third of that time.
More pipes means less time, so divide by 5 at the end.

steps.explain: 7 pipes fill 3 tanks in 45 minutes. To find the time for ONE tank, divide the time by 3.
steps.work: \(45\div3=15\text{ minutes for 7 pipes to fill 1 tank}\)

steps.explain: Now find how long ONE pipe takes. One pipe works 7 times slower than 7 pipes, so it needs 7 times as long.
steps.work: \(15\times7=105\text{ minutes for 1 pipe to fill 1 tank}\)

steps.explain: Now use 5 pipes. 5 pipes work 5 times as fast as 1 pipe, so they need one fifth of the time.

Check that the answer makes sense: 5 pipes are fewer than 7 pipes, so they should take MORE than 15 minutes. 21 minutes is bigger than 15. \(\checkmark\) Also \(5\times21=105=7\times15\) pipe-minutes per tank.

questions.stem: The sum of two numbers is 48. If the smaller number is equal to one fifth of the larger number, the numbers are
questions.hint: Draw a bar model: the smaller number is 1 equal part and the larger number is 5 of the same parts. Then 6 parts together make 48.

keyPoints.text: one fifth of the larger number
keyPoints.note: If small = 1/5 of large, then large = 5 × small, so large is 5 equal parts and small is 1 part.
The two numbers added together are 48.

questions.stem: In a public library, 30% of the books are classified as fiction and the remainder as non-fiction. There are 2400 more non-fiction books than fiction books. The number of books in the fiction category are
questions.hint: Turn the percentages into a difference: non-fiction is 70% and fiction is 30%, so the 2400 extra books are the gap between them. Use that gap to find 10%.

keyPoints.note: Fiction is 30%, so non-fiction is the remaining 100% − 30% = 70%.
2400 is the DIFFERENCE between the non-fiction and fiction numbers, not the number of fiction books.

steps.explain: Non-fiction is the remainder, so find its percentage.
The difference between non-fiction and fiction is a percentage of all the books.
This 40% is equal to the 2400 extra books.
Find 10% by dividing by 4.
Fiction is 30% = 3 lots of 10%.
Check: the whole library has \(10\times600=6000\) books, fiction 1800 and non-fiction \(6000-1800=4200\). The difference is \(4200-1800=2400\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The product of three different positive integers is 15. What is their sum?
questions.hint: List all the factors of 15, then pick three DIFFERENT ones that multiply to 15. Do not forget that 1 is a positive integer.

keyPoints.note: The three numbers must all be different, so \(1\times1\times15\) is not allowed.
Product means the numbers are multiplied together.

steps.explain: List the factors of 15: numbers that divide 15 exactly.
We need three different numbers whose product is 15. Try using 1 as one of them: the other two must multiply to 15.
Check that no other set works: \(1\times1\times15\) repeats 1 (not allowed) and any set using 15 would need the other two to multiply to 1.
The three numbers are 1, 3 and 5. Add them.

questions.hint: Split 3.44 into a whole number part and a decimal part. The two decimal places mean the decimal part is a number of hundredths. Then simplify that fraction.

keyPoints.note: A decimal with two places after the point is a number of hundredths: 0.44 = 44/100.

steps.explain: Split the number into its whole part and its decimal part.
0.44 has two decimal places, so it is 44 hundredths.
Simplify \(\dfrac{44}{100}\): divide the top and bottom by their highest common factor, 4.
Put the whole number back to make a mixed number.

Check by changing back: \(\dfrac{11}{25}=\dfrac{11\times4}{25\times4}=\dfrac{44}{100}=0.44\). \(\checkmark\) Option B, \(\dfrac{33}{25}\), equals 1.32 and option C, \(3\dfrac{11}{50}\), equals 3.22, so they are wrong.

questions.hint: “Midway” means exactly in the middle. Find the distance from A to B, halve it, then walk that half-distance from A. Take care when you cross zero.

keyPoints.note: Midway = the middle point: the same distance from A and from B.
A is on the negative side of zero. Count the distance from −4 to 6 across zero: 4 + 6 = 10.

steps.explain: Find the distance from A to B on the number line. A is 4 units left of zero and B is 6 units right of zero, so the distance crosses zero.

questions.stem: Which of the following is less than \(\dfrac{1}{6}\)?
questions.hint: Change \(\dfrac16\) into a decimal first. It goes on forever (0.1666...). Then compare each option digit by digit, writing them with the same number of decimal places.

keyPoints.note: You need a value SMALLER than 1/6 = 0.1666…, not equal to it and not bigger.

steps.explain: Change \(\dfrac16\) into a decimal by dividing 1 by 6. The decimal never stops.
Compare option A: \(0.1667\) against \(0.1666\ldots\). The first three decimal places match, then the fourth place is 7 compared with 6, so A is bigger.
Option B: simplify \(\dfrac{3}{18}\) by dividing the top and bottom by 3. It is exactly equal to \(\dfrac16\), not less.
Option C: \(0.167=0.1670\) is bigger than \(0.1666\ldots\) (third decimal 7 against 6).
Option D: \(0.1666\) stops after the four 6s, but \(\dfrac16\) keeps going \(0.16666666\ldots\), which is a little more. So D is less than \(\dfrac16\).

questions.stem: The weight of a ham and cheese sandwich is 180 grams. 40% of the weight of the sandwich is ham. How many grams of ham are there in the sandwich?
questions.hint: Find 10% first (divide by 10), then multiply to get 40%. Or write 40% as a decimal and multiply by 180.

keyPoints.note: 40% of the TOTAL weight (180 g) is ham, so multiply 180 by 40/100.

steps.explain: The whole sandwich is 100%, which is 180 grams. Find 10% by dividing by 10.
40% is four lots of 10%.
Check with decimals: write 40% as 0.4 and multiply by the weight.
Check that the rest makes sense: the other 60% is \(180-72=108\) g of bread and cheese. \(72\) is less than half of 180, which is right because 40% is less than 50%. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: After 15 games, Ben's average number of points per game was 17. After 20 games his average had increased to 21. What was his average number of points per game in the last 5 games?
questions.hint: Turn each average into a total (total = average \(\times\) number of games). The points in the last 5 games are the new total minus the old total.

keyPoints.text: average number of points per game
keyPoints.note: average × number of games = total points.
Only the LAST 5 games count: take the total after 20 games and subtract the total after 15 games.

steps.explain: After 15 games the average was 17, so Ben's total points were:
After 20 games the average was 21, so his total points were:
The points scored in the last 5 games are the difference between the two totals.
The question asks for the AVERAGE per game over those 5 games, so divide by 5.
Check: if he scored an average of 33 in 5 games, that is 165 points. Then \(255+165=420\) and \(420\div20=21\). \(\checkmark\) The number 165 is the total, not the average.

questions.stem: If \(p\) squares of each side 1 mm make a square of side 1 m, then \(p\) is equal to
questions.hint: Compare the AREAS. First find how many millimetres are in 1 metre, then remember that a square has two sides, so the number of small squares is that number multiplied by itself.

keyPoints.note: Each small square is 1 mm by 1 mm, so its area is 1 mm².
Change 1 m into millimetres before comparing areas.

steps.explain: Change the big square's side into millimetres.
Along one side of the big square we can fit 1000 small squares of side 1 mm.
The big square has 1000 rows, each with 1000 small squares.
Multiply.

Check with areas: the big square has area \(1\text{ m}^2=1\,000\,000\text{ mm}^2\) and each small square has area \(1\text{ mm}^2\), so \(1\,000\,000\div1=1\,000\,000\). \(\checkmark\) The answer 1000 would count only one row of squares.

questions.stem: If \(n\) is an odd number, which of the following must be even?
questions.hint: Test each expression with two different odd numbers, for example \(n=1\) and \(n=3\) (or 5). An expression that MUST be even gives an even answer every time.

keyPoints.note: 'Must' means always. One odd answer for any odd n is enough to rule an option out.

steps.explain: Choose some odd values of \(n\): 1, 3 and 5. Test option A, \(\dfrac{n-1}{2}\).
A gives an odd number when \(n=3\), so it does not have to be even. Now option C, \(\dfrac{n+1}{2}\).
C gives an odd number when \(n=1\), so it is not always even. Now option D, \(n^2+2n=n(n+2)\): an odd number times an odd number is odd.
Option B: \(2n+2=2(n+1)\) has a factor of 2, so it is even for every value of \(n\).
Only option B is always even.

questions.stem: Joan answered all 50 questions on a test. If she scored 78% on the test, how many questions did she get wrong?
questions.hint: 78% is the percentage she got RIGHT. Find the percentage she got wrong first, then find that percentage of the 50 questions.

keyPoints.note: 78% is how much she got RIGHT. The question asks about the wrong answers.

keyPoints.text: how many questions did she get wrong
keyPoints.note: Wrong = 100% − 78% = 22% of the 50 questions.

steps.explain: A score of 78% means she got 78% of the questions right. Find the percentage she got wrong.
Find 22% of the 50 questions. Convert 22% to a decimal (22 hundredths).
Multiply by 50.
Check the other way: 78% of 50 is \(0.78\times50=39\) right answers, and \(50-39=11\) wrong answers. \(\checkmark\) The number 39 is how many she got RIGHT.

steps.explain: All corners are right angles, so the two horizontal pieces on top together cover the same width as the bottom side.
In the same way, the two vertical pieces on the left side (9.1 m and \(c\)) together cover the same height as the right side.
Replace each pair by its total, so the perimeter equals the perimeter of the rectangle that is 19.8 m wide and 13.4 m high.
Check with another method: the missing step is \(c=13.4-9.1=4.3\) m. Adding \(a+b=19.8\) for any split of the top gives the same total.

keyPoints.note: The shape has six corners, so it is a hexagon. One corner is a “dent” (a reflex angle bigger than 180°).

keyPoints.text: All the corners are right angles
keyPoints.note: Right angles are 90°, but the inside of the dent corner measures 270° (360° − 90°).

steps.explain: A shape with \(n\) sides can be cut into \(n-2\) triangles from one corner, and each triangle has angles adding to \(180^\circ\).
Multiply the number of triangles by \(180^\circ\).
Check by adding the actual corners: five corners are \(90^\circ\) on the inside and the dent corner is \(270^\circ\) on the inside (a full turn \(360^\circ\) minus the \(90^\circ\) outside it).
Both methods agree. A rectangle has \(360^\circ\), but this shape has two more corners, so it must be more than \(360^\circ\).

questions.stem: A triangle has one 30 degree angle and one 60 degree angle. Which of the following types of triangle is it?
questions.hint: The angles of a triangle add up to 180°. Find the third angle, then compare with the definitions of each type of triangle.

keyPoints.text: one 30 degree angle and one 60 degree angle
keyPoints.note: Two angles are known, so the third angle is 180° minus their sum.

steps.explain: The three angles of any triangle add up to \(180^\circ\). Add the two known angles first.
Subtract from \(180^\circ\) to find the third angle.
The angles are \(30^\circ,\ 60^\circ,\ 90^\circ\). A triangle with a \(90^\circ\) angle is a right-angled triangle.
Check the other types: isosceles needs two equal angles (all three are different), equilateral needs three \(60^\circ\) angles, and obtuse needs an angle bigger than \(90^\circ\). None of these fits.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: In a caravan, in addition to 50 hens, there are 45 goats and 8 camels with some keepers. If the total number of feet is 224 more than the number of heads in the caravan, the number of keepers is
questions.hint: Count feet and heads separately. Hens and keepers have 2 feet; goats and camels have 4 feet. Every animal or person has exactly 1 head. Let the number of keepers be \(k\) and make an equation.

keyPoints.text: 224 more than the number of heads
keyPoints.note: feet = heads + 224. Write an expression for each side.
The number of keepers is unknown: call it k. Keepers have 2 feet and 1 head each.

steps.explain: Let \(k\) be the number of keepers. Count the heads: each hen, goat, camel and keeper has one head.
Count the feet. Hens have 2 feet, goats 4, camels 4, keepers 2.
Add: \(100+180+32=312\) feet for the animals, and \(2k\) feet for the keepers.
The feet are 224 more than the heads, so write an equation.
Simplify the right side: \(103+224=327\). Then subtract \(k\) from both sides and subtract 312.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: A tree of height 5 metres casts a shadow 8 metres long at a certain time of day. A second tree nearby casts a shadow 10 metres long at the same time. How many metres taller is the second tree than the first?
questions.hint: At the same time of day the ratio of height to shadow length is the same for every tree. Find the second tree's height first, then subtract the first tree's height (the question asks how much TALLER).

keyPoints.note: Same time of day means the sun is at the same angle, so height : shadow is the same for both trees.
The answer is a difference: second height − first height, not the second height alone.

steps.explain: At the same time, the ratio of height to shadow length is the same for both trees. For the first tree:
The shadow of the second tree is 10 m. Find the multiplier from 8 to 10 (or find the height of 1 m of shadow: \(5\div8=0.625\) m of tree for each metre of shadow).
Multiply by the second tree's shadow length.
The second tree is 6.25 m tall. The question asks how much TALLER it is than the first tree (5 m), so subtract.
Check: shadows 8 m and 10 m give a ratio of \(10\div8=1.25\), and \(5\times1.25=6.25\). \(\checkmark\) The option 6.25 m is the height of the second tree, not the difference.

P runs for exactly as long as O needs to finish 100 revolutions, so find that time first.

questions.stem: Three cubes of side 6 cm are glued together to make a rectangular box. What is the difference in the total surface area of the three separate cubes and the surface area of the rectangular box?
questions.hint: Find the surface area of the three separate cubes, then the surface area of the box they make when glued in a row (18 cm long, 6 cm wide, 6 cm high), then subtract. You can also count the faces that become hidden.

keyPoints.note: Gluing hides the faces that touch. Each glued join hides 2 faces (one from each cube).
Subtract the smaller surface area from the larger one.

steps.explain: A cube has 6 square faces. Each face is \(6\times6=36\text{ cm}^2\), so one cube has surface area:
Three separate cubes have three times as much surface area.
Glued in a row, the box measures 18 cm by 6 cm by 6 cm. Its surface area is 2 faces of \(18\times6\), 2 more faces of \(18\times6\), and 2 end faces of \(6\times6\).
Find the difference between the two surface areas.
Check by counting hidden faces: there are 2 glued joins and each hides 2 faces of \(36\text{ cm}^2\), so the box has \(4\) faces fewer than three separate cubes.

questions.stem: Which statement is not true?
options: Two perpendicular lines always form four right angles.
Diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other.
Angles sum to 180° in a triangle.
All the angles in a parallelogram are equal
questions.hint: This question asks for the statement that is FALSE. Check each one: try to draw an example that breaks it (a counter-example).

keyPoints.note: Three statements are true and ONE is false. Find the false one.

steps.explain: Statement A: perpendicular lines meet at \(90^\circ\). Where two straight lines cross they make 4 angles, and all four are right angles when the lines are perpendicular. TRUE.
Statement B: in a rhombus the two diagonals cut each other exactly in half (and cross at right angles). TRUE.
Statement C: the three angles in any triangle add up to \(180^\circ\). TRUE.

Statement D: a general parallelogram, for example a slanted one, has two acute angles and two obtuse angles. Only opposite angles are equal. For example the angles could be \(60^\circ,\ 120^\circ,\ 60^\circ,\ 120^\circ\).
The angles in a parallelogram are all equal only in the special case of a rectangle, so statement D is NOT always true.

questions.stem: A car travelling at an average rate of 54 kilometres per hour made a trip in 5 hours. If it had travelled at an average speed of 60 kilometres per hour, how many minutes less would the trip have taken?
questions.hint: The distance of the trip does not change. Find it from the first journey (distance = speed \(\times\) time), then find the new time at the faster speed and subtract. Answer in minutes!

keyPoints.note: Subtract the two times, and give the difference in MINUTES (1 hour = 60 minutes).
Distance = speed × time = 54 × 5.

steps.explain: Find the distance of the trip using distance \(=\) speed \(\times\) time.
At 60 km/h the same distance takes: time \(=\) distance \(\div\) speed.
The original trip took 5 hours, so the time saved is:
Change to minutes by multiplying by 60.
Check: 4.5 hours is 4 hours 30 minutes, and 5 hours is 30 minutes more. \(\checkmark\) The option 4.5 hours is the new time, not the time saved.

questions.stem: Jack went for a drive. Before he left, he noticed that the petrol tank was three quarters full. When he returned home, the petrol tank was one sixth full. The petrol tank holds 60 litres when completely full. How many litres of petrol did Jack use on his drive?
questions.hint: Find what FRACTION of a full tank was used (start minus end). Use a common denominator for \(\dfrac34\) and \(\dfrac16\). Then find that fraction of 60 litres.

keyPoints.note: Start: 3/4 of the tank. Use the same denominator as 1/6 to subtract.

keyPoints.text: How many litres of petrol did Jack use
keyPoints.note: Used = the fraction that disappeared × 60 litres.

steps.explain: The fraction of a full tank used is the starting amount minus the finishing amount.
Use a common denominator, 12: \(\dfrac34=\dfrac{9}{12}\) and \(\dfrac16=\dfrac{2}{12}\).
So \(\dfrac{7}{12}\) of the full tank was used. Find \(\dfrac{7}{12}\) of 60 litres: divide by 12, then multiply by 7.
Jack used 35 litres.
Check in litres: start \(\dfrac34\times60=45\) L, end \(\dfrac16\times60=10\) L, so used \(45-10=35\) L. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The average of a set of 10 numbers is 15. If one number is removed the average of the remaining numbers is 16. What is the value of the number removed?
questions.hint: Use total \(=\) average \(\times\) how many numbers, before and after the number is removed. The removed number is the difference between the two totals.

keyPoints.text: average of a set of 10 numbers is 15
keyPoints.note: Total of the 10 numbers = 15 × 10.
After removing one number there are only 9 numbers left, not 10.

steps.explain: The total of all 10 numbers is the average times 10.
After one number is removed, 9 numbers remain and their average is 16. Find their total.
The removed number is what is missing from the total.
Check: if the 6 is removed, the other nine add to 144 and \(144\div9=16\). \(\checkmark\) (Removing a small number made the average go up.)

questions.stem: Diane has \(2\dfrac12\) cans of paint that are just enough to paint \(\dfrac13\) of her room. How many more cans of paint will she need to finish her room and paint a second room of the same size?
questions.hint: Find how many cans paint ONE whole room (it is 3 thirds). Then find the cans for TWO rooms and subtract the cans she already has.

keyPoints.note: 2½ cans paint one third, so a whole room is three times as much.
Subtract the cans Diane already has from the total she needs.

steps.explain: \(2\dfrac12\) cans paint \(\dfrac13\) of the room. A whole room is 3 thirds, so multiply by 3.
She wants to paint two rooms of the same size, so double the amount.
She already has \(2\dfrac12\) cans. The number of MORE cans she needs is:
Check: \(12\dfrac12+2\dfrac12=15\) cans, which is enough for 2 rooms at \(7\dfrac12\) cans each. \(\checkmark\) The option 15 forgets the cans she already has.

questions.stem: If a dealer had sold a stereo for \(\$600\), he would have made a 20 percent profit. Instead, he sold it for a 40 percent loss. At what price was the stereo sold?
questions.hint: Profit and loss are percentages of the COST price. Use the first sentence to find the cost price (\(\$600\) is 120% of it), then take away 40% of the cost.

keyPoints.note: Selling price = cost + 20% of cost = 120% of the cost price.
A 40% loss means he sells for 60% of the COST price (not 60% of $600).

steps.explain: A 20% profit means \(\$600\) is the cost price plus 20% of the cost price, so \(\$600\) is 120% of the cost price.
Find 10% of the cost: divide by 12, then 100% by multiplying by 10.
So the cost price of the stereo was \(\$500\). A 40% loss means he sold it for 60% of the cost price.
Calculate 60% of \(\$500\).

Check: a 40% loss on \(\$500\) is \(0.4\times500=\$200\), and \(\$500-\$200=\$300\). \(\checkmark\) The option \(\$372\) wrongly takes 40% off \(\$600\) (and \(\$315\) is not a percentage of anything useful).

questions.stem: John buys 4 kilograms of cheese to feed 30 people at a party. If 50 people come to the party, how many grams of cheese must John buy in order to feed everyone at the original rate?
questions.hint: The answer must be in GRAMS, so change 4 kg to grams first. Find the cheese for ONE person (divide), then multiply by the 50 people.

keyPoints.note: 1 kg = 1000 g, so 4 kg = 4000 g. The answer must be in grams.
Same amount per person as before: 4000 g shared among 30 people.

steps.explain: The question asks for grams. Change the 4 kg of cheese into grams.
At the party, 4000 g feed 30 people. Find the cheese for ONE person by dividing.
For 50 people, multiply the amount per person by 50.
This matches option D. (Calculated value: \(\dfrac{200\,000}{30}\approx6667\) g.)

Check the other options: A uses 4 (kg, not grams) and multiplies the wrong way; B and C put the numbers on the wrong parts of the fraction and give tiny answers. More people need MORE cheese, so the answer must be bigger than 4000 g. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Oak trees line both sides of a street for a length of a kilometre. If there is 8 metres of space between the trees, and each tree is 1 metre wide, how many trees are there along the street?
questions.hint: Work with ONE side of the street first. A tree is 1 m wide and then there is an 8 m gap, so each “tree + gap” pattern is 9 m long. There is one more tree than there are gaps. Remember the street has two sides.

keyPoints.note: Two sides means the number of trees on one side must be doubled at the end.
1 kilometre = 1000 metres.

steps.explain: Change the street length to metres.
On one side, trees and gaps alternate: tree, gap, tree, gap, ..., tree. It starts and ends with a tree, so there is one more tree than gaps. Let there be \(n\) trees and \(n-1\) gaps.
Expand the bracket and collect the terms.
Divide by 9 to find the number of trees on one side.
The trees line BOTH sides of the street, so double it.
Check one side: 112 trees take 112 m and 111 gaps take \(111\times8=888\) m. \(112+888=1000\) m. \(\checkmark\) The option 112 is only one side.

questions.stem: A store offers a variety of discounts that range between 10 percent and 25 percent inclusive. If a book is discounted to a price of \(\$2.40\), what was its greatest possible price originally?
questions.hint: The sale price (\(\$2.40\)) is a percentage of the ORIGINAL price: a bigger discount means a smaller percentage is paid. To get the greatest original price, which discount (10% or 25%) should be used?

keyPoints.note: The original price is largest when the discount is largest, because the same $2.40 is then a smaller percentage of the original.
Inclusive means 25% itself is allowed, so use exactly 25%.

steps.explain: A discount of \(d\%\) means the customer pays \((100-d)\%\) of the original price. For the discounts 10% to 25%, the percentage paid is between 90% and 75%.
The original price equals \(\$2.40\) divided by the fraction paid. A SMALLER fraction paid gives a LARGER original price, so use the biggest discount, 25%, which means paying 75%.
Find 25% (one quarter) of the original: \(\$2.40\div3=\$0.80\). The whole original is four quarters.
So the greatest possible original price is \(\$3.20\).
Check the other extreme: a 10% discount gives \(\$2.40\div0.9\approx\$2.67\), which is smaller. Also \(\$3.20\) with 25% off is \(3.20-0.80=\$2.40\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A vault holds only 80-gram tablets of gold and 50-gram tablets of silver. If there are 1300 grams of gold and silver in total, what is the greatest amount of gold that can be in the vault, in grams?
questions.hint: Gold comes in lumps of 80 g, silver in lumps of 50 g, and the TOTAL must be exactly 1300 g. Try the largest number of gold tablets and check whether the leftover weight is a whole number of silver tablets.

keyPoints.note: Try the most gold tablets first, then reduce until the rest can be made from 50 g silver tablets.
The answer is a weight in grams (not the number of tablets).

steps.explain: Let \(g\) be the number of gold tablets and \(s\) the number of silver tablets. The total weight is 1300 g.
Both tablet weights are divisible by 10, so divide everything by 10 to make the numbers smaller.
Try the greatest number of gold tablets. \(130\div8=16.25\), so \(g\) is at most 16. Test \(g=16\): then \(5s=130-128=2\), which is not a whole number of tablets.
Test \(g=15\): \(8\times15=120\), so \(5s=130-120=10\) and \(s=2\) silver tablets. This works.
The greatest amount of gold is the weight of 15 gold tablets (the option 15 is the number of tablets, not the weight).
Check the total weight: gold 1200 g plus silver \(2\times50=100\) g.

questions.stem: John runs from home to school at an average speed of 6 km per hour, and then walks home along the same route at an average speed of 3 km per hour. If his whole journey took one hour, how many km is his home from his school?
questions.hint: Call the distance \(d\) km. Use time \(=\) distance \(\div\) speed for each part of the journey and make the two times add up to 1 hour.

keyPoints.note: Time running + time walking = 1 hour.
Both parts cover the same distance d, one in each direction.

steps.explain: Let the distance from home to school be \(d\) km. The time to run to school is distance divided by speed.
The walk home is the same distance at 3 km per hour.
The whole journey takes 1 hour, so add the two times.
Use a common denominator: \(\dfrac{d}{3}=\dfrac{2d}{6}\).
Multiply both sides by 2.
Check: running 2 km at 6 km/h takes 20 minutes; walking 2 km at 3 km/h takes 40 minutes. \(20+40=60\) minutes \(=1\) hour. \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: An optometrist charges \(\$300.00\) for an eye examination, frames, and glass lenses, but \(\$420.00\) for an eye examination, frames, and plastic lenses. If the plastic lenses cost four times as much as the glass lenses, how much do the glass lenses cost?
questions.hint: The examination and the frames cost the same in both bills, so they cancel when you compare the two prices. The difference \(\$120\) is entirely due to the lenses.

keyPoints.text: four times as much as the glass lenses
keyPoints.note: Plastic = 4 × glass, so the extra cost of plastic over glass is 3 times the glass lenses.
These two items appear in both bills, so they cancel in the difference.

steps.explain: Both bills include the same eye examination and frames. The only difference between them is the lenses. Subtract the two bills.
Let the glass lenses cost 1 part. Plastic lenses cost 4 parts, so plastic costs \(4-1=3\) parts more than glass.
The extra \(\$120\) is equal to 3 parts, so find 1 part.
One part is the cost of the glass lenses.
Check: plastic lenses cost \(4\times\$40=\$160\), and \(\$160-\$40=\$120\), the difference between the two bills. \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.hint: First find \(x\): write 81 as a power of 3 by multiplying 3 by itself until you reach 81. Then cube that value of \(x\).

keyPoints.note: x is the POWER (exponent): the number of 3s multiplied together to make 81.
The question wants x cubed (x × x × x), not x itself and not 3 cubed.

steps.explain: Find the power of 3 that gives 81 by repeated multiplication.
So \(3^x=81=3^4\), which means \(x=4\).
The question asks for \(x^3\), so cube 4 (multiply 4 by itself three times).
Calculate: \(4\times4=16\) and \(16\times4=64\).
Check: \(3^4=81\) \(\checkmark\). The option 81 is \(3^x\) itself, and 27 (\(3^3\)) is not an option; the answer needs \(4^3\), not \(3^4\).

questions.stem:
Here is some information about pupils in a class.

- The total number of pupils is 30
- 26 of the pupils do not wear glasses.
- A quarter of the pupils who do wear glasses are boys.
- There are 2 more boys than girls.

Use the information to find the fraction of girls who wear glasses in the class.
questions.hint: Fill in a two-way table (boys/girls against glasses/no glasses) one clue at a time. Then read the question carefully: “in the class” means the fraction is out of the WHOLE class of 30 pupils.

keyPoints.text: fraction of girls who wear glasses in the class
keyPoints.note: Read as: the girls who wear glasses, as a fraction of the whole class (30 pupils).

keyPoints.text: A quarter of the pupils who do wear glasses are boys
keyPoints.note: First find how many pupils wear glasses, then take a quarter of that number for the boys.

steps.explain: Pupils who wear glasses: 26 do NOT wear glasses, out of 30, so the rest do.

questions.stem: What number must be added to both numerator and the denominator of the fraction \(\dfrac{7}{15}\) to change its value to \(\dfrac{3}{5}\)?
questions.hint: Let the unknown number be \(x\). The new fraction is \(\dfrac{7+x}{15+x}\). Set it equal to \(\dfrac35\) and cross-multiply. You can also test each option by adding it to the top and bottom.

keyPoints.text: added to both numerator and the denominator
keyPoints.note: The SAME number is added to the top and to the bottom: (7 + x)/(15 + x).

steps.explain: Let \(x\) be the number added to both the numerator and the denominator.
Cross-multiply (multiply each numerator by the other fraction's denominator).
Expand both brackets.
Subtract \(3x\) and 35 from both sides.
Check: add 5 to the top and bottom of \(\dfrac{7}{15}\).

questions.stem: Minh misses the bus to school 2 days out of 5 days. He leaves his Mathematics textbook at home 3 days out of 4. What is the probability of Minh catching the bus with his Mathematics text book?
questions.hint: You need BOTH events to happen: he catches the bus AND he has his textbook. First find the probability of each event (be careful: the question gives the chances of the “bad” events), then multiply.

keyPoints.text: misses the bus to school 2 days out of 5 days
keyPoints.note: If he misses the bus 2 days in 5, he CATCHES it on the other 3 days in 5.

keyPoints.text: leaves his Mathematics textbook at home 3 days out of 4
keyPoints.note: If he leaves it 3 days in 4, he TAKES it only 1 day in 4.

steps.explain: He misses the bus 2 days out of 5, so he catches the bus on the other 3 days out of 5.
He leaves the textbook at home 3 days out of 4, so he has the textbook on only 1 day out of 4.
He needs both things to happen on the same day, and the two events do not affect each other, so multiply the two probabilities.
Change \(\dfrac{3}{20}\) to a percentage: multiply the top and bottom by 5 to get a denominator of 100.
Check the other options: 85% is the chance he does NOT manage both (\(100\%-15\%\)), and 30% or 23% do not come from \(\dfrac35\times\dfrac14\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.hint: Make both numbers the same type. Change \(\dfrac34\) into a decimal (divide 3 by 4), then subtract the decimals, lining up the decimal points.

keyPoints.note: The first number is a mixed number and the second is a decimal. Convert one so both are decimals.

steps.explain: Change the fraction part into a decimal. \(\dfrac34\) means \(3\div4\), or three quarters, which is 0.75.
Now subtract. Line up the decimal points and subtract column by column.
Subtract the hundredths \(5-2=3\), the tenths \(7-3=4\), and the ones \(6-6=0\).
Check by adding back: the answer plus 6.32 should give 6.75.

questions.hint: Add the four decimals first (line up the decimal points), then change the answer into a mixed number. Remember \(0.5=\dfrac12\).

keyPoints.note: Add all four decimals, then convert the total to a mixed number to match the options.

steps.explain: Write every number with three decimal places so the columns line up.
Add the first two numbers, then the other two.
Add the two results.
Change 1.5 into a mixed number: the whole part is 1 and the decimal part 0.5 is one half.
Check with fractions: \(\dfrac18+\dfrac14+\dfrac38+\dfrac34=\dfrac{1+2+3+6}{8}=\dfrac{12}{8}=1\dfrac12\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Using the digits 1, 2, 5, 9 exactly once in each number, what is the difference between the second largest and the second smallest number that can be formed?
questions.hint: Build the biggest numbers by putting the largest digits in the highest places, and the smallest numbers by putting the smallest digits first. List the top two and bottom two, then subtract.

keyPoints.text: second largest and the second smallest
keyPoints.note: Not the largest or smallest! List the two largest and the two smallest numbers carefully.
Each number uses all four digits 1, 2, 5, 9, each exactly once.

steps.explain: For the largest numbers, put the biggest digit first: 9, then 5, then 2, then 1. The largest is 9521. The second largest swaps the last two digits.
For the smallest numbers, put the smallest digit first: 1, then 2, then 5, then 9. The smallest is 1259. The second smallest swaps the last two digits.
Now subtract the second smallest from the second largest.
Subtract column by column (borrowing where needed): \(9512-1000=8512\), \(8512-295=8217\).
Check: \(8217+1295=9512\). \(\checkmark\) Using the largest and smallest instead would give \(9521-1259=8262\), which is a trap answer.

questions.stem: A typist can type 45 words per minute. He then increases his speed by 20 percent. How many words can he now type per hour?
questions.hint: First find his new speed in words per minute (add 20% of 45 to 45). The question asks per HOUR, so multiply by 60 minutes at the end.

keyPoints.note: Increase by 20% means the new speed is 120% of the old speed (old speed + 20% of it).
The final answer must be words per HOUR, not per minute: multiply by 60.

steps.explain: Find 20% of 45. 10% is 4.5, so 20% is double that.
His new speed is the old speed plus the increase.
There are 60 minutes in an hour, so multiply by 60.
Calculate: \(54\times6=324\), so \(54\times60=3240\).
Check: 45 words per minute is \(45\times60=2700\) words per hour, and 20% more is \(2700\times1.2=3240\). \(\checkmark\) The option 2700 is the speed before the increase.

questions.stem:
The integers A, B, and C are consecutive and \(A\lt B\lt C\). If \(A^2=C\), which of the following could be the value of A?

I. \(-1\)
II. \(0\)
III. \(2\)
questions.hint: Consecutive integers go up by 1 each time, so if the first is A then B is \(A+1\) and C is \(A+2\). Test each given value of A in the rule \(A^2=C\).

keyPoints.note: Consecutive integers: each is exactly 1 more than the one before (A, A + 1, A + 2).

keyPoints.text: could be the value of A
keyPoints.note: Test each of I, II and III separately; more than one can work.

steps.explain: Consecutive integers increase by 1, so \(B=A+1\) and \(C=A+2\). The rule \(A^2=C\) becomes \(A^2=A+2\).
Test I, \(A=-1\): the numbers are \(-1,\ 0,\ 1\) and \(C=1\). Is \(A^2=C\)?
Test II, \(A=0\): the numbers are \(0,\ 1,\ 2\) and \(C=2\). Is \(A^2=C\)?
Test III, \(A=2\): the numbers are \(2,\ 3,\ 4\) and \(C=4\). Is \(A^2=C\)?
I and III work; II does not. So the answer is “I and III only”.

questions.stem: The length of a rectangle is \(\dfrac27\) of the perimeter. What is the area of the rectangle if the perimeter is 14 centimetres?
questions.hint: Find the length first (two sevenths of 14). The perimeter is TWO lengths plus TWO widths, so after you take away the two lengths you can find the width. Finally multiply length by width.

keyPoints.note: Perimeter = 2 × length + 2 × width. Do not forget there are two of each.
Area of a rectangle = length × width.

steps.explain: Find the length: \(\dfrac27\) of the perimeter 14 cm. Divide by 7, then multiply by 2.
The perimeter has two lengths and two widths. Take away the two lengths from 14.
Share the 6 cm between the two widths.
Area \(=\) length \(\times\) width.
Check the perimeter: \(2\times4+2\times3=8+6=14\) cm. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem:
What one value for \(x\) can be correctly entered into the equation below?

\(\dfrac{2+3}{x}=\dfrac{2+x}{3}\)
questions.hint: Simplify the left top \(2+3\) first, then test each option by putting it in for \(x\) on both sides and checking they are equal. Or cross-multiply.

keyPoints.note: Only ONE of the four options makes both sides equal. Test each option.

steps.explain: Simplify the top of the left fraction.
Test option A, \(x=7\): left \(=\dfrac57\), right \(=\dfrac{9}{3}=3\). They are not equal.
Test options B and C: \(x=10\) gives \(\dfrac{5}{10}=\dfrac12\) and \(\dfrac{12}{3}=4\); \(x=8\) gives \(\dfrac58\) and \(\dfrac{10}{3}\). Neither pair is equal.
Test option D, \(x=3\): left \(=\dfrac53\) and right \(=\dfrac{2+3}{3}=\dfrac53\). They are equal.
Check by cross-multiplying: \(5\times3=x(2+x)\), so \(x^2+2x-15=0\), which factorises as \((x+5)(x-3)=0\). So \(x=3\) (the other solution, \(-5\), is not an option).

questions.stem: 230 people at a party decide to order pizza for a snack. If each pizza has 8 slices, how many pizzas should they order so that each person can have one slice?
questions.hint: Divide the number of people by the number of slices per pizza. If there is a remainder, you still need one more pizza because pizzas cannot be bought in parts.

keyPoints.text: each person can have one slice
keyPoints.note: Everyone needs a slice, so a leftover group of people still needs another pizza.

keyPoints.text: how many pizzas should they order
keyPoints.note: Pizzas come whole: round UP when there is a remainder.

steps.explain: Each pizza has 8 slices and each person needs 1 slice, so divide 230 by 8.
28 pizzas give \(28\times8=224\) slices, which is enough for only 224 people. 6 people would have no slice.
So one more pizza is needed for the last 6 people.
Check: 29 pizzas give \(29\times8=232\) slices, enough for 230 people (2 slices spare). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The number for eight million, ninety thousand, twenty and one hundredth is
questions.hint: Write each part in its own place-value column and use 0 as a placeholder for any empty column. One hundredth is the second place after the decimal point.

keyPoints.note: The first decimal place is tenths and the second is hundredths, so one hundredth is 0.01, not 0.1.
Ninety thousand = 90 000, so the 9 goes in the ten-thousands column.

steps.explain: Write the value of each part of the number.
Set out a place-value chart: millions 8, hundred-thousands 0, ten-thousands 9, thousands 0, hundreds 0, tens 2, ones 0, tenths 0, hundredths 1. Use zeros for empty places.
Write the digits in order with the decimal point after the ones digit.
Check the wrong options: 8 090 020.10 has one TENTH (0.1) instead of one hundredth; 8 900 020.10 has 900 thousand instead of 90 thousand; 8 900 200.01 has both 900 thousand and 200. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: In a class of 21 students, the ratio of boys to girls is 4: 3. Some extra boys and one extra girl join the class. The new ratio becomes 3:2. What is the number of new boys joined?
questions.hint: First find the number of boys and girls in the original class (the ratio 4 : 3 has 7 parts). Then the new number of girls tells you the new number of boys from the ratio 3 : 2.

keyPoints.text: ratio of boys to girls is 4: 3
keyPoints.note: 4 parts boys and 3 parts girls: 7 parts altogether make the 21 students.
Only ONE extra girl joins, so the new number of girls is easy to find.

steps.explain: The ratio 4 : 3 has \(4+3=7\) parts, and 7 parts are 21 students. Find one part.
Find the original number of boys and girls.
One extra girl joins, so the new number of girls is:
The new ratio of boys to girls is 3 : 2, so 2 parts are 10 girls. Find one part, then the 3 parts of boys.
The number of NEW boys is the new total minus the 12 boys who were already there.
Check: the new class has 15 boys and 10 girls, and \(15:10=3:2\). \(\checkmark\) The option 15 is the total number of boys now, not the new boys.

questions.stem: A charity organisation sells greetings cards in packs costing \(\$10\) or \(\$5\) each. A total of 75 packs were sold at a fair for a total of \(\$625\). How many of the \(\$5\) packs were sold?
questions.hint: Pretend ALL 75 packs were the dearer \(\$10\) packs and see how much too much money that would be. Each \(\$5\) pack that replaces a \(\$10\) pack lowers the total by \(\$5\). Or use guess and check.

keyPoints.note: Number of \(\$10\) packs + number of \(\$5\) packs = 75.
The question asks for the number of the CHEAPER \(\$5\) packs, not the \(\$10\) packs.

steps.explain: Suppose all 75 packs cost \(\$10\). The total would be:
The actual total is \(\$625\), which is less. Find the difference.
Every time one \(\$10\) pack is replaced by a \(\$5\) pack, the total goes down by \(\$5\). So the number of \(\$5\) packs is the difference divided by 5.
So 25 packs cost \(\$5\) and the other \(75-25=50\) packs cost \(\$10\).
Check the total: \(50\times\$10+25\times\$5=\$500+\$125=\$625\). \(\checkmark\) The option 50 is the number of \(\$10\) packs.

questions.stem: Andy, Mark and Sean all have their birthdays today, but Andy is more than twice as old as Mark and Mark is more than four years older than Sean. If Andy is less than 16 years old, what is one possible value for Sean's age in years?
questions.hint: Test each option for Sean's age. For each, find the SMALLEST whole-number age Mark could have (more than 4 years older than Sean), then the smallest age Andy could have (more than twice Mark). Andy must still be under 16.

keyPoints.text: more than twice as old as Mark
keyPoints.note: Andy's age is bigger than 2 × Mark's age (strictly bigger).

keyPoints.text: more than four years older than Sean
keyPoints.note: Mark's age is bigger than Sean's age + 4 (strictly bigger).
Andy must be 15 or younger (ages are whole numbers).

steps.explain: Test Sean \(=2\): Mark must be more than \(2+4=6\), so Mark is at least 7. Andy must be more than \(2\times7=14\), so Andy is at least 15, which is less than 16.
Test Sean \(=3\): Mark must be more than \(3+4=7\), so at least 8. Andy must be more than \(2\times8=16\), so at least 17, which is NOT less than 16.
Test Sean \(=4\): Mark at least 9, so Andy at least 19. Too old.
Test Sean \(=5\): Mark at least 10, so Andy at least 21. Too old.
Older values for Sean make Mark and Andy even older, so only Sean \(=2\) works.

Count how many 40-minute periods fit into 200 minutes.
Write the population after each doubling (as a multiple of the start): \(\times2\), \(\times4\), \(\times8\), \(\times16\), \(\times32\).
The population is multiplied by 2 five times.
Check: the option 5 comes from adding 5 doublings instead of multiplying; doubling means multiplying by 2 each time. \(\checkmark\)

keyPoints.note: The three pairs are 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4.
Look for straight strips of three squares: the two end squares are opposite faces.

steps.explain: On the die, opposite faces add to 7, so the pairs are \((1,6)\), \((2,5)\), \((3,4)\).

Now the top row: the face with 4 dots, B and C form a straight strip. The first and third faces are opposite, so C is opposite the 4-dot face.
The only face left to pair is B, which must be opposite the 1-dot face (the only face not yet matched).
The answer is \(A=2\), \(B=6\), \(C=3\). Check that the pairs are \((2,5)\), \((6,1)\), \((3,4)\) and use all of 1 to 6 exactly once. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A school charity sale raised \(\$4800\). One quarter of this was taken to cover expenses. Three quarters of the remainder was given to Charity A and the remainder to Charity B. How much did B receive?
questions.hint: Do the fractions one step at a time, always checking what the “remainder” is. Three quarters of the REMAINDER (not of the \(\$4800\)) goes to Charity A.

keyPoints.text: One quarter of this was taken to cover expenses
keyPoints.note: A quarter of the whole \(\$4800\) goes on expenses.
Three quarters of what is LEFT after expenses, not of the \(\$4800\).

steps.explain: Find the expenses: one quarter of \(\$4800\).
Find the remainder after the expenses.
Charity A gets three quarters of the remainder.
Charity B gets the rest of the remainder, which is the other quarter.
Check: \(\$1200+\$2700+\$900=\$4800\). \(\checkmark\) The option \(\$2700\) is what Charity A receives.

questions.stem: A brush salesman earns \(\$50\) salary each month plus 10 percent commission on the value of his sales. If he earned \(\$200\) last month, what was the total value of his sales?
questions.hint: Take the fixed salary away from his earnings to find the commission. The commission is 10% of the sales, so the sales are 10 times the commission.

keyPoints.text: \(\$50\) salary each month plus 10 percent commission
keyPoints.note: Earnings = salary + commission. Take the salary off first.

keyPoints.text: the total value of his sales
keyPoints.note: Commission is 10% of the SALES, so sales = commission ÷ 10%.

steps.explain: His earnings are the salary plus the commission. Find the commission by taking the salary away.
The commission is 10% of the sales, so \(\$150\) is 10% of the value of his sales. Find 100%: multiply by 10.
Calculate.

questions.stem: During a season in a certain baseball league, every team plays every other team ten times. If there are ten teams in the league, how many games are played altogether in the league in one season?
questions.hint: First count how many DIFFERENT pairs of teams there are (each pair is one match-up, so do not count A v B and B v A separately). Then multiply by 10 because each pair meets ten times.

keyPoints.text: every team plays every other team ten times
keyPoints.note: Each PAIR of teams plays 10 games against each other.
Count each pair of teams only once.

steps.explain: Each of the 10 teams plays 9 other teams. If we multiply, every pair is counted twice (A against B is the same pair as B against A).
Divide by 2 to count each pair once.
Each pair of teams plays 10 games against each other.
Check with the pattern: \(9+8+7+6+5+4+3+2+1=45\) pairs, and \(45\times10=450\) games. \(\checkmark\) The option 900 counts each pair twice.

Test the options. 0.45 kg is between 0.25 and 0.5, so it is on this step.
0.65 kg is on the next step (cost about \(\$5\)), and 1.75 kg and 3.75 kg are on steps costing more than \(\$5.50\). They do not cost \(\$3.75\).
So the parcel could have a mass of 0.45 kg.

The rectangles cover the part that is NOT empty, so subtract.
The 12 rectangles are all the same size, so divide the area by 12.

Check with the sizes: the frame is \((50-40)\div2=5\) cm thick, so each rectangle is 5 cm wide. Along one side there are three rectangles that, together with one rectangle width, span 50 cm: \(3\times l+5=50\), so \(l=15\) cm. Area \(=15\times5=75\) cm\(^2\). \(\checkmark\)

steps.explain: The number of squares goes up by 3 for each extra octagon, so the rule starts with \(3\times\) (number of octagons). Test: for 1 octagon \(3\times1=3\) but there are 4 squares, so we must add 1.
Check the rule with another row: 4 octagons gives \(3\times4+1=13\) squares. \(\checkmark\)
Now the pattern has 121 squares. Put 121 into the rule and undo the \(+1\) by subtracting 1.
Undo the multiplication by dividing by 3.
Check: \(3\times40+1=121\). \(\checkmark\) The option 364 is \(3\times121+1\), which wrongly uses 121 as the number of octagons.

questions.stem: P stands for a multiple of 3. Q stands for a different multiple of 3. Which statement is not true?
options: The difference between P and Q is a multiple of 3.
The product of P and Q is a multiple of 9.
The quotient of P and Q is a not always multiple of 3.
The sum of P and Q is a multiple of 6.
questions.hint: Test every statement with real examples, such as \(P=3\) and \(Q=6\) or \(P=6\) and \(Q=9\). A statement is NOT true if even one example breaks it. Careful: statement C already says “not always”.

keyPoints.note: Three statements are true. Find the one that fails for at least one example.
P and Q are two different numbers from 3, 6, 9, 12, ...

steps.explain: Write a multiple of 3 as \(3a\) and another as \(3b\) (where \(a\) and \(b\) are different whole numbers). Test statement A, the difference: \(3a-3b=3(a-b)\), which is a multiple of 3. TRUE.
Statement B, the product: \(3a\times3b=9ab\), which is a multiple of 9. TRUE.
Statement C: the quotient is not always a multiple of 3. For example \(6\div3=2\) is not a multiple of 3. So the statement “not always a multiple of 3” is TRUE.
Statement D, the sum: \(3a+3b=3(a+b)\) is a multiple of 3, but it is a multiple of 6 only if \(a+b\) is even. Try \(P=3\) and \(Q=6\).
steps.work: \(3+6=9\), which is not a multiple of 6

steps.explain: Statement D fails for this example, so it is the statement that is NOT true.

questions.stem: A 25 litre solution is 20 percent alcohol. If 50 litres of water are added to it, what percent of the new solution is alcohol?
questions.hint: The amount of alcohol does NOT change when you add water, but the total volume does. Find the litres of alcohol first, then divide by the new total volume.

keyPoints.note: 20% of the 25 litres is alcohol. That amount stays the same.
The new total volume is 25 + 50 litres.

steps.explain: Find the amount of alcohol in the original solution.
Adding water does not add any alcohol, so there are still 5 litres of alcohol. Find the new total volume.
The percentage of alcohol is the alcohol divided by the total volume, times 100%.
Simplify \(\dfrac{5}{75}=\dfrac{1}{15}\), then multiply by 100: \(100\div15=6\dfrac23\).
Check: the new solution is three times as big (75 L against 25 L), so the percentage must be \(20\%\div3=6\dfrac23\%\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: There are 567 students in a school. \(\dfrac47\) are boys and the rest are girls. There are 9 times as many girls as there are teachers. How many teachers are there?
questions.hint: Find the fraction of the school that are girls (1 minus \(\dfrac47\)), then the number of girls. The number of teachers is the number of girls divided by 9.

keyPoints.note: Girls = the whole school minus the boys: 1 − 4/7 = 3/7.

keyPoints.text: 9 times as many girls as there are teachers
keyPoints.note: girls = 9 × teachers, so teachers = girls ÷ 9.

steps.explain: The boys are \(\dfrac47\) of the students, so the girls are the remaining part.
Find the number of girls: divide 567 by 7, then multiply by 3.
There are 9 times as many girls as teachers, so divide the girls by 9.
Check: \(27\times9=243\) girls. The boys are \(81\times4=324\), and \(324+243=567\). \(\checkmark\) The option 243 is the number of girls.

steps.explain: Find how much \(y\) drops in each step.
The drops are NOT equal, so the graph is not a straight line. This rules out D (a straight line).

The drops get smaller and smaller, so the graph falls steeply at first and then flattens out. This is the curve in graph C. Graph A does the opposite: it starts flat and falls more steeply at the end.
Check with the ratios: each value is about a third of the previous one (\(43\div120\approx0.36\), \(15\div43\approx0.35\), \(5.5\div15\approx0.37\)), which is a decaying curve. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The breadths of two rectangles, X and Y, have measurements of 14 cm and 8 cm. The sum of the lengths of X and Y is 22 cm and the sum of their area is \(236\text{ cm}^2\). What is the area of X?
questions.hint: Rectangle X has breadth 14 cm and Y has breadth 8 cm (in that order). Let the length of X be \(x\), so the length of Y is \(22-x\). Write each area as breadth \(\times\) length and make the two areas add to 236.

keyPoints.text: The sum of the lengths of X and Y is 22 cm
keyPoints.note: If X has length x, then Y has length 22 − x.

keyPoints.text: What is the area of X?
keyPoints.note: Area of X = 14 × (length of X). Find the length of X first.

steps.explain: Let the length of X be \(x\) cm. The lengths add to 22 cm, so the length of Y is \(22-x\).
Area \(=\) breadth \(\times\) length. Write the area of each rectangle.
The two areas add to 236.
Expand the bracket and collect the \(x\) terms.

Check: Y has length \(22-10=12\) cm and area \(8\times12=96\) cm\(^2\). The total is \(140+96=236\) cm\(^2\). \(\checkmark\) The option 96 is the area of Y.

questions.stem: If 30 jellybeans cost you \(\$5\), which one is not the expression of how many jellybeans you can purchase for \(\$17\)?
questions.hint: Find how many jellybeans one dollar buys. Then evaluate each option (or simplify it) and see which one gives a DIFFERENT answer from the others.

keyPoints.text: which one is not the expression
keyPoints.note: Three expressions give the correct number of jellybeans and ONE does not. Find the odd one out.
Jellybeans for \(\$17\) = (jellybeans per dollar) × 17.

steps.explain: Find how many jellybeans \(\$1\) buys: 30 jellybeans cost \(\$5\), so divide 30 by 5.
For \(\$17\) the correct number is 17 times as many.
Option A: dividing by \(\dfrac{5}{30}\) is the same as multiplying by \(\dfrac{30}{5}=6\). Option C is also \(17\times\dfrac{30}{5}=17\times6\).
Option B: \(17\times\dfrac{500}{3}\) is about \(17\times166.7=2833\), which is much bigger. It does not match.
So B is the expression that is NOT correct.

questions.stem: In our car, it took us 15 minutes to cover 18 km. At this rate, how long would it take to travel 210 km?
questions.hint: First find the speed in km per HOUR (15 minutes is a quarter of an hour). Then time \(=\) distance \(\div\) speed, and change the decimal part of the hours into minutes.

keyPoints.note: 15 minutes is one quarter of an hour, so the car covers 4 × 18 km in one hour.
Time = distance ÷ speed. The answer must be in hours and minutes.

steps.explain: 15 minutes is a quarter of an hour, so in a whole hour the car travels 4 times as far.
Time \(=\) distance \(\div\) speed.
Divide: 72 goes into 210 twice (144), leaving 66. So the time is 2 hours and \(\dfrac{66}{72}\) of an hour.
Change \(\dfrac{11}{12}\) of an hour into minutes: \(\dfrac{11}{12}\times60\).
The journey takes 2 hours 55 minutes.
Check with another method: 210 km is \(\dfrac{210}{18}=11\dfrac23\) lots of 18 km. Each lot takes 15 minutes: \(11\dfrac23\times15=175\) minutes \(=2\) h 55 min. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: In a box, there are 28 red beads, 16 green beads and 20 yellow beads. Express the number of green beads as a fraction of the total number of red and yellow beads.
questions.hint: The fraction compares green beads with the red AND yellow beads only (not with all the beads in the box). Add the red and yellow beads first, then write green over that total and simplify.

keyPoints.text: as a fraction of the total number of red and yellow beads
keyPoints.note: The bottom of the fraction is red + yellow only. Green beads are NOT included in the total.

steps.explain: Find the total number of red and yellow beads.
Write the number of green beads over this total.
Simplify by dividing top and bottom by the highest common factor, 16.
Check: one third of 48 is 16, the number of green beads. \(\checkmark\) (If you wrongly used all 64 beads you would get \(\dfrac{16}{64}=\dfrac14\).)

questions.stem: My average result from the last 4 maths exams was 28 out of 40. What do I need in my fifth exam in order to increase my average by 2?
questions.hint: The new average must be 28 + 2 = 30 over FIVE exams. Use total \(=\) average \(\times\) number of exams to find the totals before and after, and subtract.

keyPoints.note: New average = 28 + 2 = 30 (an increase of 2, not a score of 30 in the exam).
The average is then over 5 exams, so the new total is 5 × the new average.

steps.explain: The total of the first 4 exams is the average times 4.
The new average is 2 more than 28.
With 5 exams and an average of 30, the total must be:
The fifth exam score must make up the difference.
Check: \(112+38=150\) and \(150\div5=30\), which is 2 more than 28. \(\checkmark\) A score of 38 out of 40 is possible.

questions.stem: Suppose P and Q both represent prime numbers such that \(5\times P+7\times Q=109\). Find the value of P and Q.
questions.hint: A prime number has exactly two factors (1 and itself). First cross out any option that contains a number that is not prime, then test the rest in the equation.

keyPoints.note: 12 is not prime (it has factors 2, 3, 4, 6), so options with 12 can be ruled out immediately.
Put P first and Q second from each option into the equation.

steps.explain: A prime number has only two factors. 12 can be divided by 2, 3, 4 and 6, so 12 is NOT prime. This rules out options A (12, 7) and B (5, 12).
Test option C: \(P=7\), \(Q=5\).
Test option D: \(P=19\), \(Q=2\). Both are prime numbers.
Add.
Only option D satisfies the equation, so \(P=19\) and \(Q=2\).

questions.stem: Three people share a sum of money in the ratio of 6 : 4 : 3. The person who receives the least amount get \(\$270\). Find the total amount of money they shared.
questions.hint: The smallest number in the ratio, 3, goes with the person who gets the least. Use that to find the value of one part, then multiply by the total number of parts.

keyPoints.note: The least amount matches the smallest ratio number, 3 parts.

keyPoints.text: total amount of money they shared
keyPoints.note: Total = all the parts together: 6 + 4 + 3 parts.

steps.explain: The person with the least money has the smallest share, 3 parts, and receives \(\$270\). Find the value of one part.
Find the total number of parts.
Multiply the number of parts by the value of one part.
Check the shares: \(6\times90=540\), \(4\times90=360\), \(3\times90=270\). \(540+360+270=1170\). \(\checkmark\) The options 3510 and 1620 come from using the wrong number of parts.

questions.stem: If \(m\) is an odd number, which of the numbers below must be odd?
questions.hint: Remember: odd \(\times\) odd \(=\) odd, and odd \(\pm\) 1 \(=\) even. Test each option with an odd number such as \(m=3\) and \(m=5\).

keyPoints.note: 'Must' means it is odd for EVERY odd value of m. One even result rules the option out.

steps.explain: Test option A, \(2\times m\): any number multiplied by 2 is even.
Test option B, \(3\times m+1\): odd times odd is odd, and odd plus 1 is even.
Test option C, \((m-1)\times(m+1)\): both brackets are even (odd minus 1 and odd plus 1), so the product is even.
Test option D, \(m^2=m\times m\): odd times odd is always odd.
Only option D is always odd.

questions.stem: Multimedia Messaging Service, or MMS, is a standard way to send messages that contain multimedia content to and from mobile phones. Every student in an eighth grade class sends an MMS to each of the other students in the class. There are 210 messages. How many students are there in the class?
questions.hint: If there are \(n\) students, each student sends a message to \(n-1\) others. So the number of messages is \(n\times(n-1)\). Look for two consecutive numbers that multiply to 210, or test the options.

keyPoints.note: Each student sends to everyone EXCEPT themselves, so n − 1 messages each.
The total number of messages is n × (n − 1) = 210.

steps.explain: Let the class have \(n\) students. Each student sends one message to each of the other \(n-1\) students.
All \(n\) students do this, so the total number of messages is:
Look for two consecutive whole numbers that multiply to 210. Try numbers near \(\sqrt{210}\approx14.5\): \(14\times13=182\) (too small) and \(15\times14=210\).
Check the other options: 14 students gives \(14\times13=182\), 12 gives \(132\), and 17 gives \(272\). Only 15 gives 210. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Peter can eat a pizza in 4 minutes. Jim can eat a pizza in 5 minutes. Their dad can eat a pizza in 20 minutes. If two boys and dad all start eating the same pizza at the same time, how long does it take them to finish one pizza?
questions.hint: Work out how many pizzas each person eats in the same length of time, such as 20 minutes (the lowest common multiple of 4, 5 and 20). Add them to find the pizzas eaten by all three together.

keyPoints.text: all start eating the same pizza at the same time
keyPoints.note: They eat together, so add their eating rates.

keyPoints.text: Peter can eat a pizza in 4 minutes
keyPoints.note: In 20 minutes Peter eats 20 ÷ 4 pizzas.

steps.explain: Choose a time that 4, 5 and 20 all divide into: 20 minutes. In 20 minutes, Peter eats \(20\div4\) pizzas.
In 20 minutes Jim eats \(20\div5\) pizzas, and Dad eats \(20\div20\) pizza.
Together they eat this many pizzas in 20 minutes.
So one pizza takes one tenth of 20 minutes.
Check with fractions of a pizza per minute: \(\dfrac14+\dfrac15+\dfrac1{20}=\dfrac{5+4+1}{20}=\dfrac{10}{20}=\dfrac12\) of a pizza per minute, so a whole pizza takes 2 minutes. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The total weight of Chris and his sister Ann is 157 kilograms. Chris's weight is 1 kilogram more than twice Ann's weight. What is Ann's weight?
questions.hint: Let Ann's weight be \(x\). Then Chris's weight is \(2x+1\). Their weights add to 157. A bar model also works: Ann is 1 part, Chris is 2 parts and 1 extra kilogram.

keyPoints.text: 1 kilogram more than twice Ann's weight
keyPoints.note: Chris = 2 × Ann + 1. First double Ann's weight, THEN add 1.
The answer is Ann's weight, not Chris's.

steps.explain: Let Ann's weight be \(x\) kg. Twice her weight is \(2x\), so Chris weighs 1 kg more than that.
Their total weight is 157 kg.
Collect the \(x\) terms: \(x+2x=3x\).
Subtract 1 from both sides, then divide by 3.
Check: Chris weighs \(2\times52+1=105\) kg and \(52+105=157\) kg. \(\checkmark\) The option 78 is half of 156 and does not fit the clue about Chris.

questions.hint: Do the multiplication on the top first (ignore the decimal points, then count the decimal places), then divide by 0.002. Or write each number as a power of ten times a whole number.

keyPoints.note: Work out the top (numerator) first, then divide the result by the bottom number.

steps.explain: Multiply the top numbers without the decimal points: \(2\times3=6\).
Count the decimal places: 0.02 has 2 and 0.0003 has 4, so the product has \(2+4=6\) decimal places.
Now divide by 0.002. Write the numbers as whole numbers times powers of ten: \(0.000006=6\times10^{-6}\) and \(0.002=2\times10^{-3}\).
\(3\times10^{-3}\) means 3 thousandths.
Check by multiplying back: the answer times the bottom number must give the top number.

questions.stem: Which of the following has the greatest value?
questions.hint: Write every number with three decimal places (add zeros on the end) and compare place by place from the left: tenths first, then hundredths, then thousandths.

keyPoints.note: Compare tenths first, then hundredths. A longer decimal is NOT always bigger: 0.15 is bigger than 0.145.

steps.explain: Write all four numbers with three decimal places so that they have the same length. 0.15 becomes 0.150.
Compare the tenths digits: all four numbers have 1 tenth, so they tie.
Compare the hundredths digits: 0, 4, 3 and 5. The greatest hundredths digit is 5.
So 0.150 is the greatest. Remember 0.15 \(=\) 0.150.
Check: \(0.150-0.145=0.005\gt0\), so 0.15 is bigger than 0.145 even though 0.145 has more digits. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: \(1+\dfrac12+\dfrac14+\dfrac16+\dfrac18=\)
questions.hint: Find a common denominator for 2, 4, 6 and 8. The smallest number that all of them divide into is 24. Write every term over 24 (including the 1).

keyPoints.note: Do not forget the whole number 1: it is \(\dfrac{24}{24}\) when the denominator is 24.

steps.explain: Find the lowest common multiple of the denominators 2, 4, 6 and 8. Multiples of 8: 8, 16, 24. Check 24 is also a multiple of 2, 4 and 6.
Change each term into 24ths by multiplying the top and bottom by the same number.
Add the numerators (the denominators stay the same).
Check with decimals: \(1+0.5+0.25+0.1667+0.125\approx2.04\), and \(\dfrac{49}{24}=2.04\ldots\). \(\checkmark\) Options A, B and C are all less than 2, so they leave out some terms.

questions.stem: On a map 1 centimetre represents 100,000 centimetres. What is the length of a road in kilometres that measures 2.9 centimetres on the map?
questions.hint: First change 100 000 cm into kilometres (100 cm = 1 m, 1000 m = 1 km). Then 1 cm on the map is that many kilometres, so multiply by 2.9.

keyPoints.note: That is the scale: every 1 cm on the map is 100 000 cm in real life.
The answer must be in km, so convert from centimetres.

steps.explain: Convert 100 000 cm to metres: divide by 100.
Convert 1000 m to kilometres: divide by 1000.
So 1 cm on the map represents 1 km in real life. The road measures 2.9 cm on the map.

questions.stem: 60 percent of what number is equal to 45 percent of 80?
questions.hint: Work out 45% of 80 first. Then ask: 60% of which number gives that answer? Divide by 0.6.

keyPoints.note: Find this value first: it is the target number.
The unknown number is the whole (100%), so divide the target by 60% = 0.6.

steps.explain: Find 45% of 80. Convert 45% to the decimal 0.45 and multiply.
Now 60% of the unknown number \(N\) must equal 36.
Divide both sides by 0.6.
Check: 60% of 60 is \(0.6\times60=36\), and 45% of 80 is 36. \(\checkmark\)

steps.explain: Net D has only 3 triangles, so it cannot be folded into the pyramid. Net D is wrong.

Net B has 4 triangles, but two of them are on top of the square and two are on the right. The left side and the bottom side of the square have no triangle at all (and the extra triangles would overlap when folded). Net B is wrong.
steps.work: \(B:\ \text{two triangles on the top edge, two on the right}\ \times\)

steps.explain: In net A the strip of 4 triangles is attached to the square through just one triangle. The triangle on the far left does not touch the point where the other three triangles meet, so it cannot join the apex. Net A is wrong.
steps.work: \(A:\ \text{one triangle does not reach the apex}\ \times\)

steps.explain: In net C the first triangle is attached to the square, and the other three triangles are attached to each other around ONE point. All four triangles share this point, which becomes the apex when folded, so C folds into a square-based pyramid.

questions.stem: In which of the following are the diagonals of the figure always congruent and perpendicular?
questions.hint: Congruent diagonals means the two diagonals have the SAME length. Perpendicular means they cross at \(90^\circ\). Think about which shape needs BOTH properties: rectangle-like (equal diagonals) AND rhombus-like (perpendicular diagonals).

keyPoints.note: BOTH properties must hold for every example of the shape.
An equilateral triangle has no diagonals at all (it has only 3 vertices).

steps.explain: Parallelogram: the diagonals bisect each other, but they are usually not equal in length and not perpendicular. Not always both.
Rhombus: the diagonals are perpendicular, but they are not equal unless the rhombus is a square (a long thin rhombus has one long and one short diagonal).
Equilateral triangle: a triangle has only 3 vertices, so there are no diagonals to compare.
Square: the diagonals have the same length (it is a rectangle) AND cross at \(90^\circ\) (it is a rhombus). Both properties hold for every square.
Check with a square of side 1: both diagonals have length \(\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt{2}\), so they are equal, and they cross at right angles. \(\checkmark\)
