questions.stem: A violinist practices one hour a day from Monday through Friday. How many hours must she practice on Saturday in order to have an average of two hours a day for the six-day period?
questions.hint: Use total \(=\) average \(\times\) number of days. Find the total practice time she needs over 6 days, subtract what she has already done in 5 days, and the rest must be done on Saturday.

keyPoints.text: average of two hours a day for the six-day period
keyPoints.note: Monday to Saturday is SIX days, so the total needed is 2 × 6 hours.

keyPoints.text: one hour a day from Monday through Friday
keyPoints.note: That is 5 days of 1 hour each = 5 hours so far.

steps.explain: Find the total practice time needed over the six days (Monday to Saturday) for an average of 2 hours.
She has already practised 1 hour on each of 5 days.
The rest must be done on Saturday.
Check: \(5+7=12\) hours over 6 days, and \(12\div6=2\) hours per day. \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: In a sequence of numbers the first number is 3 and the 5th number is 39. What number could be the 12th number in this sequence?
questions.hint: Assume the numbers go up by the SAME amount each time (the common difference). From the 1st to the 5th term there are 4 steps. Find the size of one step, then count 11 steps from the 1st term to the 12th.

keyPoints.text: the first number is 3 and the 5th number is 39
keyPoints.note: Between the 1st and 5th number there are 4 equal steps, not 5.
From the 1st to the 12th number there are 11 steps.

steps.explain: From the 1st number to the 5th number there are 4 steps (the 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 5th). The total increase is:
If each step adds the same amount, divide the total increase by the number of steps.
The sequence is 3, 12, 21, 30, 39, ... It grows by 9 each time.
From the 1st to the 12th number there are 11 steps of 9.
Add to the first number.
Check with the rule \(\text{term}=9\times\text{position}-6\): the 1st is \(9-6=3\), the 5th is \(45-6=39\), the 12th is \(108-6=102\). \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: The school library has 5 action adventure novels, 15 romances and 10 historical novels. Julie wants to take one of each type for her sick cousin to read. How many different choices of three books are available to her?
questions.hint: She picks ONE book from each of three groups. Every choice from the first group can be combined with every choice from the second group, and so on, so multiply the numbers of choices (not add).

keyPoints.note: She chooses one action book AND one romance AND one historical novel, so the choices multiply.
Count each different set of three books.

steps.explain: There are 5 choices for the action adventure novel.
For EACH of those 5 choices she can pick any of the 15 romances. Count the choices for the first two books together.
For each of these 75 pairs she can choose any of the 10 historical novels.
Check the wrong answers: \(5+15+10=30\) is what you get if you ADD the numbers (that counts the number of books, not the number of choices of three). \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: If a sack of dried dog food feeds 4 dogs or 5 puppies for one week, then 5 sacks of the same food will feed 15 puppies and how many dogs?
questions.hint: One sack feeds 5 puppies, so find how many sacks the 15 puppies use. The sacks that are left over feed dogs, 4 dogs per sack.

keyPoints.note: One sack feeds EITHER 4 dogs OR 5 puppies for a week.
There are 5 sacks to share between the puppies and the dogs.

steps.explain: One sack feeds 5 puppies. Find how many sacks are needed for 15 puppies.
There are 5 sacks altogether. Find how many sacks are left for the dogs.
One sack feeds 4 dogs, so 2 sacks feed:
Check by finding a fraction of a sack: each puppy eats \(\dfrac15\) of a sack and each dog \(\dfrac14\) of a sack. \(15\times\dfrac15+8\times\dfrac14=3+2=5\) sacks. \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: In a test a student got a mark of 49. His report card showed that he had scored 70 per cent. What was the maximum mark on the test?
questions.hint: 49 is 70% of the maximum mark. Find 10% by dividing 49 by 7, then find 100%.

keyPoints.note: 49 marks is 70% of the TOTAL marks available. The maximum is the 100% amount.

steps.explain: Let the maximum mark be \(M\). He scored 70% of it, which is 49 marks.
70% is 7 lots of 10%, so find 10% by dividing 49 by 7.
The maximum mark is 100%, which is 10 lots of 10%.
Check: 70% of 70 is \(0.7\times70=49\). \(\checkmark\) The maximum mark must be more than his mark of 49.

questions.stem: If it takes ten minutes to fill \(\dfrac{5}{12}\) of a hole, how many minutes will it take to fill the rest of the hole at the same rate?
questions.hint: Find what fraction of the hole is LEFT to fill. Then find how long it takes to fill one twelfth, and multiply.

keyPoints.note: 5/12 is already filled in 10 minutes. The rest is the other 7/12.
The rate is constant, so equal fractions of the hole take equal times.

steps.explain: Find the fraction of the hole that is left. The whole hole is \(\dfrac{12}{12}\).
\(\dfrac{5}{12}\) takes 10 minutes. Find the time to fill one twelfth by dividing by 5.
The remaining \(\dfrac{7}{12}\) is 7 twelfths, so multiply by 7.
Check: the whole hole takes \(12\times2=24\) minutes, and \(24-10=14\) minutes. \(\checkmark\) The option 24 is the time for the whole hole.

questions.stem: A butcher buys 20 kilograms of beef for \(\$380\). If 10 percent of the beef is unusable, at approximately what average price per kilogram must he sell the rest of the beef in order to make a profit of 25 percent?
questions.hint: Find the selling income he needs: cost plus 25% profit. Then find how many kilograms he can actually sell (only 90% is usable) and divide the income by that mass.

keyPoints.text: 10 percent of the beef is unusable
keyPoints.note: He can only sell 90% of the 20 kg. The unusable beef is still paid for.
A profit of 25% means he must collect 125% of what he paid, \(\$380\).

steps.explain: Find the mass of beef he can sell. 10% is unusable, so 90% can be sold.
Find the total money he must receive for a 25% profit on his cost of \(\$380\). The total must be 125% of the cost.
Share the \(\$475\) between the 18 kg that can be sold.
Divide: \(18\times26=468\), leaving 7, so \(475\div18\approx26.39\), which is about \(\$26.40\).
Check: \(18\times26.40=\$475.20\approx\$475\), which is a 25% profit on \(\$380\). \(\checkmark\) The option \(\$23.75\) comes from \(475\div20\), which wrongly sells all 20 kg.

questions.stem: The sum of the lengths of all the roads in county Z is 1,400 km. If the sum of the lengths of unpaved roads is \(\dfrac34\) the sum of the lengths of paved roads, how many more kilometres of paved roads than unpaved are there in county Z?
questions.hint: Unpaved \(=\dfrac34\) of paved, so paved : unpaved \(=4:3\). Use a ratio (parts) to split the 1400 km, then find the DIFFERENCE between paved and unpaved.

keyPoints.text: \(\dfrac34\) the sum of the lengths of paved roads
keyPoints.note: Unpaved is three quarters of paved: if paved is 4 parts, unpaved is 3 parts.

keyPoints.text: how many more kilometres of paved roads than unpaved
keyPoints.note: Answer = paved − unpaved (a difference), not the paved roads alone.

steps.explain: Let the paved roads be 4 parts. Three quarters of that is 3 parts, so the unpaved roads are 3 parts.
Together they are \(4+3=7\) parts, and all the roads add up to 1400 km. Find one part.
Find the length of each type of road.
The question asks how many MORE kilometres of paved than unpaved, so subtract.
Check: \(\dfrac34\) of 800 is 600 \(\checkmark\), and \(800+600=1400\). \(\checkmark\) (The difference is just 1 part: \(4-3=1\) part \(=200\) km.)

questions.stem: Which reason can be used to prove that a parallelogram is a rhombus?
questions.hint: A rhombus is a parallelogram with 4 equal sides. Ask of each reason: is it true for EVERY parallelogram (then it cannot make it special), and does it force the sides to be equal? Think about which special property only a rhombus has.

keyPoints.text: prove that a parallelogram is a rhombus
keyPoints.note: The reason must be something EXTRA that ordinary parallelograms do not always have.

steps.explain: Every parallelogram already has opposite sides parallel and opposite angles equal. Those facts cannot prove that it is a rhombus because ordinary slanted parallelograms have them too.
Option A: congruent (equal) diagonals make a parallelogram a RECTANGLE, not a rhombus. A long rectangle has equal diagonals but unequal sides.

Option D: if the diagonals of a parallelogram are perpendicular, then each diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other. Every point on it is the same distance from the two ends, which forces all four sides to be equal. So the parallelogram is a rhombus.
So the reason that proves a parallelogram is a rhombus is that its diagonals are perpendicular.

steps.explain: 150 people started the walk. The number who have left is the starting number minus the number still walking.
Write the fraction: people who left over all the walkers.
Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by 10, then by 5.

Check: the fraction still walking is \(\dfrac{80}{150}=\dfrac{8}{15}\), and \(\dfrac{7}{15}+\dfrac{8}{15}=1\). The option \(\dfrac{8}{15}\) is the fraction still walking, not the fraction who left. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem:
A, B and C stand for three different numbers.
The average of A and B is 40.
The average of B and C is 35.
\(A+B+C=100\).
Calculate the values of A, B and C.
questions.hint: Turn each average into a total: average \(\times\) 2. Then use the three totals together. Subtracting a total from \(A+B+C=100\) finds the missing letter.

keyPoints.text: The average of A and B is 40
keyPoints.note: Average of two numbers = their sum ÷ 2, so A + B = 2 × 40.
Subtract A + B from this to find C, and subtract B + C to find A.

steps.explain: The average of A and B is 40, so their sum is twice 40.
The average of B and C is 35, so their sum is twice 35.
All three add to 100. Subtract \(A+B\) to find C.
Subtract \(B+C\) from 100 to find A.
Now B is the rest: \(A+B=80\), so \(B=80-30\).
Check all conditions: \(\dfrac{30+50}{2}=40\) \(\checkmark\), \(\dfrac{50+20}{2}=35\) \(\checkmark\), \(30+50+20=100\) \(\checkmark\).

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Andrew had \(\dfrac23\) as much money as Jeremy. He gave \(\$24\) to Jeremy, who now has \(\$240\). How much money did Andrew have at the beginning?
questions.hint: The fraction \(\dfrac23\) compares Andrew's money to Jeremy's money AT THE BEGINNING (before the \(\$24\) was given). Find Jeremy's money at the beginning first.

keyPoints.note: This is the comparison at the BEGINNING, before any money was given.
\(\$240\) is Jeremy's money AFTER he received \(\$24\).

steps.explain: Jeremy now has \(\$240\) after receiving \(\$24\) from Andrew. Find what Jeremy had at the beginning by taking the gift away.
At the beginning Andrew had \(\dfrac23\) as much as Jeremy. Find \(\dfrac23\) of \(\$216\): divide by 3, then multiply by 2.
So Andrew had \(\$144\) at the beginning.

Check: Andrew \(144\) and Jeremy \(216\) have the ratio \(2:3\) \(\checkmark\). After the gift Jeremy has \(216+24=240\) \(\checkmark\). The option \(\$72\) is one third of Jeremy's money, not two thirds.

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: The area of a rectangle is \(24\text{ cm}^2\) and the perimeter is 22cm. What is the ratio of the length to the width?
questions.hint: Half the perimeter is length + width. Find two numbers that add to 11 and multiply to 24. Then write the two numbers as the ratio. Use the options to decide the order.

keyPoints.text: The area of a rectangle is
keyPoints.note: Area = length × width, so the two sides multiply to 24.
Perimeter = 2 × (length + width), so the two sides add up to 22 ÷ 2 = 11.

steps.explain: The perimeter is twice the sum of the two sides, so the two sides add up to half of 22 cm.
The area is the product of the two sides.
Find two numbers that multiply to 24 and add to 11. List the factor pairs of 24: \(1\times24\), \(2\times12\), \(3\times8\), \(4\times6\). The pair \(3\) and \(8\) adds to 11.
The sides are 3 cm and 8 cm. Of the options, the only ratio made from these two numbers is \(3:8\) (so the question's “length : width” is \(3:8\), with the 3 cm side listed first).
Check the other options: \(2:3\) and \(1:6\) would need sides like 2 and 3 or 1 and 6, which do not give area 24 and perimeter 22. \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: In a test there were 120 questions. Leanne answered 85% of the questions and obtained a score of 80%. How many of the questions she answered were incorrect?
questions.hint: Find (a) how many questions she answered and (b) how many she got right (score \(80\%\) of ALL 120 questions). The questions she answered but got wrong are the difference.

keyPoints.note: She attempted 85% of the 120 questions. The others she did not answer at all.
The score is 80% of the whole test (120 questions): that is the number she got right.

steps.explain: Find how many questions she answered: 85% of 120.
Find how many she got right: a score of 80% of the 120 questions.
The incorrect answers are among the questions she answered, so subtract the correct from the answered.
Check by percentages: she answered 85% and got 80% right, so \(85\%-80\%=5\%\) of 120 were wrong: \(0.05\times120=6\). \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Lucy took 20 minutes to cycle from school to her home at an average speed of 12 km/h. If she wanted to reach home 5 minutes early, what must her average speed be?
questions.hint: Find the distance first (distance \(=\) speed \(\times\) time, with the time in hours). Then find the new time, 5 minutes less, and use speed \(=\) distance \(\div\) time.

keyPoints.note: The speed is in km per HOUR, so change 20 minutes into hours: 20 ÷ 60 = 1/3 hour.
The new time is 20 − 5 = 15 minutes.

steps.explain: Change 20 minutes to hours: 20 minutes is one third of an hour.
Find the distance from school to home: distance \(=\) speed \(\times\) time.
She wants to arrive 5 minutes early, so the new time is 15 minutes, which is a quarter of an hour.
New speed \(=\) distance \(\div\) time.
Check: at 16 km/h, 4 km takes \(4\div16=\dfrac14\) hour \(=15\) minutes. \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: If the value of \(X\) and \(Y\) in the fraction \(\dfrac{X}{Y}\) are both tripled, how does the value of the fraction change?
questions.hint: Replace \(X\) by \(3X\) and \(Y\) by \(3Y\) and simplify. You can also try a number example such as \(\dfrac23\).

keyPoints.note: BOTH the top and the bottom are multiplied by 3, not just one of them.

steps.explain: Tripling means multiplying by 3. The new fraction has \(3X\) on the top and \(3Y\) on the bottom.
Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by the common factor 3.
Try a number example: \(X=2\) and \(Y=3\) give \(\dfrac23\). Triple both: \(\dfrac{6}{9}\). Divide the top and bottom of \(\dfrac69\) by 3.
The value of the fraction is unchanged. (Multiplying the top and bottom by the same number gives an equivalent fraction.)

questions.stem: If the length of a rectangle is 20% greater than the side of a square and the breadth is 20% less than the side of the square, which one of the following statements is correct?
options: The area of the rectangle is greater than the area of the square
The area of the rectangle is equal to the area of the square
The perimeter of the rectangle is greater than the perimeter of square
The area of the rectangle is less than the area of the square
questions.hint: Choose an easy side for the square, such as 10 units. Find the length (20% more) and the breadth (20% less) of the rectangle, then compare both the areas and the perimeters.

keyPoints.text: 20% greater than the side of a square
keyPoints.note: Length = side + 20% of the side = 1.2 × side.

keyPoints.text: 20% less than the side of the square
keyPoints.note: Breadth = side − 20% of the side = 0.8 × side.

steps.explain: Let the side of the square be 10. The rectangle's length is 20% greater: \(10+2=12\). The rectangle's breadth is 20% less: \(10-2=8\).

questions.stem: A laboratory has 55 rabbits, some white and the rest brown. Which of the following could be the ratio of white rabbits to brown rabbits in the lab?
questions.hint: A ratio such as \(a:b\) splits the rabbits into \(a+b\) equal parts. The number of rabbits (55) must divide exactly by the total number of parts, otherwise you would need fractions of rabbits. Check each option's total.

keyPoints.note: 55 must be a whole-number multiple of the total number of parts (a + b).
Test each option; only one gives whole numbers of rabbits.

steps.explain: For a ratio \(a:b\) the total number of parts is \(a+b\). The 55 rabbits must be shared into whole numbers, so \(a+b\) must divide 55 exactly. The factors of 55 are 1, 5, 11 and 55.
Option A \(1:3\) has \(1+3=4\) parts, and 4 is not a factor of 55.
Option C \(5:11\) has \(5+11=16\) parts and option D \(3:4\) has 7 parts. Neither 16 nor 7 divides 55.
Option B \(3:8\) has \(3+8=11\) parts, and \(55\div11=5\) rabbits per part.
Find the numbers: white \(=3\times5=15\), brown \(=8\times5=40\).

questions.stem: A frog climbs 3 metres up a well each day and slips 2 metres down the well each night. If it takes the frog 12 days to reach the top of the well, then the greatest height of the well in metres would be
questions.hint: Each full day and night the frog makes progress of only 1 metre. On the LAST day it reaches the top during the day, so it does not slip back. Count carefully what height it reaches on the 12th day.

keyPoints.text: slips 2 metres down the well each night
keyPoints.note: Net progress each full day and night = 3 − 2 = 1 metre.
The 12th day's climb must reach the top, but the 11th day's climb must NOT have reached the top.

steps.explain: Each day he climbs 3 m and each night he slips back 2 m, so after each full day and night his height goes up by:
At the start of the 12th day he has completed 11 full days and nights, so his height is:
On the 12th day he climbs 3 m and reaches the top, so the top of the well is at most:

Check that he does not get out on day 11: at the start of day 11 he is at \(10\) m, and climbing 3 m takes him to 13 m. So if the well were 13 m or less he would have reached the top on day 11. The well must be more than 13 m and at most 14 m, so the greatest height is 14 m.

questions.stem: A rectangular farm is 12 hectares in area. If its length is 120 metres, what is the width?
questions.hint: Change hectares into square metres first (1 hectare \(=10\,000\text{ m}^2\)). Then width \(=\) area \(\div\) length. Look at the units in the options: metres and kilometres!

keyPoints.note: 1 hectare = 10 000 m² (a square 100 m by 100 m).
Width = area ÷ length. Change the answer to match the options (m or km).

steps.explain: Change hectares into square metres. One hectare is a square of side 100 m.
Find the area of the farm in square metres.
Area \(=\) length \(\times\) width, so width \(=\) area \(\div\) length.
Change to kilometres: 1000 m is 1 km.
Check: \(120\text{ m}\times1000\text{ m}=120\,000\text{ m}^2=12\) hectares. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: If \(812\times2.9=2354.8\), what do you get if 23548 is divided by 8.12?
questions.hint: Compare the numbers in the new calculation with the numbers in the given one: 23548 is 2354.8 with the decimal point moved, and 8.12 is 812 with the decimal point moved. Count how many places each moved.

keyPoints.note: Use the given answer: do not recalculate. Look at how the digits are the same but the decimal point has moved.
Dividing by a smaller number (8.12 instead of 812) makes the answer bigger.

steps.explain: From the given multiplication, divide both sides by 812: \(2.9=2354.8\div812\). So dividing 2354.8 by 812 gives 2.9.
Compare 23548 with 2354.8: the decimal point moved one place right, so 23548 is 10 times as big.
Compare 8.12 with 812: the decimal point moved two places left, so 8.12 is one hundredth of 812.
Dividing by a number 100 times smaller makes the answer 100 times larger. So the new answer is \(2.9\) times 10 times 100.
Check by multiplying back: \(2900\times8.12=23\,548\). Since \(2900\times8=23\,200\) and \(2900\times0.12=348\), the total is \(23\,548\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A car runs 6 km on 500mL of petrol. What is the cost of petrol to travel 390 km if petrol costs \(\$1.28\) per litre?
questions.hint: Find how many 6 km trips fit into 390 km, then the number of 500 mL lots of petrol. Change millilitres to litres (1 L = 1000 mL) before multiplying by the price per litre.

keyPoints.note: Every 6 km the car uses 500 mL = 0.5 L of petrol.
The price is per LITRE, so change the 500 mL to litres.

steps.explain: Find how many lots of 6 km are in 390 km.
Each 6 km uses 500 mL \(=0.5\) litres of petrol. Find the total petrol used.
The petrol costs \(\$1.28\) per litre.
Check: 12 km uses 1 L, so 390 km uses \(390\div12=32.5\) L. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Which of the following expressions is equal to the value of \((10\times100)\times(20\times80)\)?
questions.hint: Work out each bracket first: \(10\times100\) and \(20\times80\). Then compare with the options, or use the idea that multiplication can be done in any order.

keyPoints.note: Evaluate the brackets first, then compare the values of the options.

steps.explain: Work out the first bracket.
Work out the second bracket.
Multiply the two results.
Work out option A: \(2000\times800=1\,600\,000\). This is the same.

The other options are far too big: B is \(1.6\times10^9\), C is \(16\,000\,000\), and D is \(160\,000\,000\). Multiplication can be done in any order, so regroup the four numbers: pair \(100\) with \(20\), and \(10\) with \(80\).

questions.stem: Joe works as a waiter and is normally paid \(\$600\) for a 30-hour week. For how many hours would he have work in a week where his total pay is \(\$750\) if all overtime is paid at the time and a half rate?
questions.hint: Find his normal hourly rate first, then the overtime rate (time and a half \(=1.5\times\) normal rate). The extra pay above \(\$600\) is all overtime pay.

keyPoints.note: Normal pay for 30 hours: find the pay for ONE hour.
Overtime hours pay 1.5 times the normal hourly rate.

steps.explain: Find his normal hourly rate.
Overtime is paid at time and a half, which is 1.5 times the normal rate.
His normal 30 hours earn \(\$600\). The extra money in the \(\$750\) week is for overtime.
Find the overtime hours.
Total hours worked \(=\) normal hours \(+\) overtime hours.
Check: \(30\times20+5\times30=600+150=\$750\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Anna reads an average of three books per month. She takes a break and does not read any books in August. What is the total number of books that Anna reads in one year?
questions.hint: She reads 3 books in each month she reads. How many months in a year does she actually read? August is a break month, so take it away from the 12 months.

keyPoints.text: does not read any books in August
keyPoints.note: August is a break month: she reads 0 books, so only 11 months count.

keyPoints.text: an average of three books per month
keyPoints.note: She reads 3 books in each of the months she reads.

steps.explain: There are 12 months in a year. Take away August, the month with no reading.
In each of these 11 months she reads 3 books.
Multiply.
Check: \(12\times3=36\) would be the total if she read every month, and she misses 3 books in August: \(36-3=33\). \(\checkmark\)

keyPoints.note: Both rectangles are as wide as the square, and their heights add up to the side of the square.
A rectangle's perimeter is 2 × (length + width).

questions.stem: Three apples and five oranges cost \(\$8.50\), and five apples and three oranges cost \(\$8.30\). How much will it cost to buy one apple?
questions.hint: Add the two shopping lists: you get 8 apples and 8 oranges, so you can find the cost of 1 apple plus 1 orange. Then use the lists to see how apples and oranges compare.

keyPoints.text: Three apples and five oranges cost
keyPoints.note: First shopping list: 3a + 5o = 8.50.

keyPoints.text: five apples and three oranges cost
keyPoints.note: Second shopping list: 5a + 3o = 8.30.

steps.explain: Let an apple cost \(a\) dollars and an orange cost \(o\) dollars. Write the two shopping lists as equations.
Add the two equations. The total is 8 apples and 8 oranges.
Divide everything by 8 to find one apple plus one orange.
Now subtract the first list from the second list: 2 more apples and 2 fewer oranges cost \(8.30-8.50=-0.20\), so the oranges are dearer.
Use \(a+o=2.10\) and \(o=a+0.10\) to find the apple.
Check: the orange costs \(\$1.10\). First list: \(3\times1.00+5\times1.10=3+5.50=\$8.50\) \(\checkmark\). Second list: \(5\times1.00+3\times1.10=5+3.30=\$8.30\) \(\checkmark\).

questions.stem: Two hundred percent more than 30 is
questions.hint: “More than” means you ADD the increase to the original number. Find 200% of 30 first, then add it to 30.

keyPoints.note: '200% more than 30' = 30 + 200% of 30. It is NOT just 200% of 30.

steps.explain: Find 200% of 30. 100% of 30 is 30, so 200% is double that.
“200% more than 30” means 30 plus this increase.
Check: 90 is \(300\%\) of 30 (the original 100% plus 200% more): \(3\times30=90\). \(\checkmark\) The option 60 is only 200% OF 30, not 200% MORE than 30.

questions.stem: What would result in the largest number?
questions.hint: Work out the value of every option. Do the powers first (\(10^3\) means \(10\times10\times10\), and \(1^5=1\)), then add or subtract. Compare the answers.

keyPoints.note: Calculate each option fully, then compare the four values.

steps.explain: Option A: \(10^3=10\times10\times10=1000\), then subtract 310.
Option B: add 104 and 410.
Option C: \(1^5=1\times1\times1\times1\times1=1\), then add 510.
Option D: \(10^2=100\), then add 210.
Compare the four values: 690, 514, 511 and 310. The largest is 690.

questions.stem: Two and three quarter hours equals ______ minutes.
questions.hint: Change the hours into minutes: 1 hour is 60 minutes. Remember that three quarters of an hour is 45 minutes.

keyPoints.note: 2¾ hours = 2 hours + ¾ of an hour.

steps.explain: Change 2 hours into minutes.
Three quarters of an hour is three quarters of 60 minutes.
Add the two parts.
Check: \(2.75\times60=165\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.hint: Follow the order of operations: do the brackets first, then the power (square).

keyPoints.note: Brackets first: 7 − 3. The square applies to the answer of the bracket.

steps.explain: Work out the bracket first.
Now square the result: multiply it by itself.
Calculate.
Check the common mistake: \(7^2-3^2=49-9=40\) is a different calculation, because squaring does not apply to each number separately.

questions.stem: Only one of the following equals 8. Which is it?
questions.hint: Use BODMAS: Brackets, Orders, then Division and Multiplication, then Addition and Subtraction. Work out each option carefully, one at a time.

keyPoints.text: Only one of the following equals 8
keyPoints.note: Calculate every option; only one gives 8.

steps.explain: Option A, no brackets: do the multiplication and division before the addition.
Option B: brackets first. \(7\times7+7=49+7=56\). Then divide by 7.
Option C: bracket first, \(7+7=14\). Then \(7\times14=98\), then divide by 7.
Option D: inside the bracket, divide first: \(7\div7=1\), then \(7+1=8\), then multiply by 7.
Only option B equals 8.

questions.stem: What is the greatest integer that will always evenly divide the sum of three consecutive even integers?
questions.hint: Try some examples of three consecutive even numbers (such as 2, 4, 6 and 4, 6, 8) and add them. Or call the middle one \(n\): the three numbers are \(n-2\), \(n\), \(n+2\).

keyPoints.note: The divisor must work for EVERY set of three consecutive even integers, not just one example.
Among the numbers that always divide the sum, pick the greatest.

steps.explain: Let the middle even number be \(n\). The three consecutive even integers are \(n-2\), \(n\) and \(n+2\). Add them: the \(-2\) and \(+2\) cancel.
Since \(n\) is even, write \(n=2k\) for some integer \(k\). The sum becomes:
So the sum is always a multiple of 6, which means 6 always divides it evenly.
Test with examples: \(2+4+6=12\) and \(4+6+8=18\) are both divisible by 6, and 6 is the greatest number that divides both 12 and 18.
The options 2 and 4 are not the greatest. The option 5 does not divide 12. So the answer is 6.

questions.stem: If the average of 8, 11, 25, and \(p\) is 15, then \(8+11+25+p=\)?
questions.hint: You do NOT need to find \(p\). The question asks for the SUM of the four numbers. Use sum \(=\) average \(\times\) number of values.

keyPoints.note: The question asks for the total of all four numbers, which is what an average is built from.

steps.explain: The average of 4 numbers is their sum divided by 4.
Multiply both sides by 4 to find the sum.
Calculate.
Check by finding \(p\): \(8+11+25=44\), so \(p=60-44=16\). The four numbers 8, 11, 25, 16 add to 60 and \(60\div4=15\). \(\checkmark\) The option 16 is the value of \(p\), not the sum.

questions.stem: On a scaled map, a distance of 10 centimetres represents 5 kilometres. If a street is 750 metres long, what is its length on the map, in centimetres?
questions.hint: Use the same units for both distances. Change 5 km into metres, find how many metres 1 cm on the map stands for, then divide 750 m by that.

keyPoints.note: That is the scale. Change kilometres to metres before comparing with the 750 m street.
The street's real length is in metres, but the scale uses kilometres.

steps.explain: Change 5 km into metres.
10 cm on the map is 5000 m, so find how many metres 1 cm stands for.
The street is 750 m long, so divide by 500 m per cm.
Check: \(1.5\text{ cm}\times500=750\text{ m}\). \(\checkmark\) The map length is much smaller than the real length, so 15 cm would be too big.

questions.stem:
What is the value of \(u\) in this equation?

\(5\times u-10=u+46\)
questions.hint: Get all the \(u\) terms on one side and all the plain numbers on the other. Do the same thing to both sides each time (balance method).

keyPoints.note: The unknown u appears on both sides. Move the u terms to one side first.

steps.explain: The equation is \(5u-10=u+46\). Subtract \(u\) from both sides to collect the \(u\) terms on the left.
Add 10 to both sides to get the \(u\) term alone.
Divide both sides by 4.
Check by substituting \(u=14\) in both sides: left side \(5\times14-10=70-10=60\); right side \(14+46=60\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A farmer travelled a distance of 61 km in 9 hours. He travelled partly on foot at 4 km/hr and partly on bicycle at 9 km/hr. The distance travelled on foot is:
questions.hint: Suppose he cycled the WHOLE 9 hours: how far would he go? That is too far by some amount. Each hour he walks instead of cycling takes away \(9-4=5\) km. Or guess and check the number of hours on foot.

keyPoints.text: partly on foot at 4 km/hr and partly on bicycle at 9 km/hr
keyPoints.note: Foot time + bicycle time = 9 hours in total.
Answer = 4 × (hours on foot), not the number of hours.

steps.explain: If he cycled for all 9 hours, he would travel:
The real distance is 61 km, which is less. Find the difference.
Each hour spent walking instead of cycling reduces the distance by \(9-4=5\) km. So the number of hours on foot is:
Distance on foot \(=\) speed \(\times\) time.
Check: he cycled \(9-4=5\) hours covering \(5\times9=45\) km. Total \(16+45=61\) km. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem:
An old map has the following instruction for some treasures.
Stand next to the black rock and face West.
Walk 20 metres and then turn 90 degrees clockwise.
Walk another 10 metres and then turn 45 degrees anticlockwise.
Walk another 15 metres, reverse your direction and walk 5 metres back.
Turn 135 degrees clockwise and walk another 10 metres.

In which direction are you now facing?
questions.hint: Only the TURNS change the direction you face (the walking does not). Start facing West and follow each turn in order. Clockwise turns go West \(\to\) North \(\to\) East \(\to\) South. Use bearings (North \(=0^\circ\), East \(=90^\circ\), South \(=180^\circ\), West \(=270^\circ\)) to keep track.

keyPoints.note: West is a bearing of 270° (North = 0°, East = 90°, South = 180°, West = 270°).
Reversing means turning 180°.

steps.explain: Use bearings measured clockwise from North. West is \(270^\circ\). The walking distances do not change the direction, so only keep track of the turns.

Reverse your direction: turn \(180^\circ\). \(315^\circ+180^\circ=495^\circ\), and subtracting a full turn \(360^\circ\) gives \(135^\circ\), so you face South-East.
Turn \(135^\circ\) clockwise: \(135^\circ+135^\circ=270^\circ\), which is West.

questions.stem: A lighthouse blinks regularly 5 times a minute. A neighbouring lighthouse blinks regularly 4 times a minute. If they blink simultaneously, after how many seconds will they blink together again?
questions.hint: Find how many seconds there are between blinks for each lighthouse. They blink together again at the lowest common multiple (LCM) of the two times.

keyPoints.note: A minute has 60 seconds, so the gap between blinks is 60 ÷ 5 seconds.
They coincide at the first time that is a multiple of BOTH gaps: the LCM.

steps.explain: The first lighthouse blinks 5 times in 60 seconds, so one blink every:
The second lighthouse blinks 4 times in 60 seconds, so one blink every:
List the times when each blinks. First: 12, 24, 36, 48, 60, ... Second: 15, 30, 45, 60, ...
The first time they match is 60 seconds, the lowest common multiple of 12 and 15.
Check: in 60 seconds the first blinks \(60\div12=5\) times and the second \(60\div15=4\) times, both exactly. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: In a certain factory with 2,700 workers, \(\dfrac13\) of the workers are unskilled. If 600 of the unskilled workers are apprentices, what fraction of the unskilled workers are not apprentices?
questions.hint: Find the number of unskilled workers first. The fraction asked for is out of the UNSKILLED workers (not all 2700). Subtract the apprentices to get those who are not apprentices.

keyPoints.note: Unskilled workers = one third of 2700.

keyPoints.text: what fraction of the unskilled workers
keyPoints.note: The denominator is the number of unskilled workers, not the whole factory.

steps.explain: Find the number of unskilled workers: one third of 2700.
600 of these unskilled workers are apprentices. Find how many are not apprentices.
Write the fraction of the UNSKILLED workers who are not apprentices.
Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by 300.
Check: \(\dfrac13\) of 900 is 300 and the apprentices are \(\dfrac23\) of 900, which is 600. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Mr Lim drove at 70 km/h for 1 hour 30 minutes. He then drove another 55 km. If his average speed for the whole journey was 80 km/h, what was his speed for the last 55 km of his journey?
questions.hint: Find the total distance and use the average speed to find the total time. Subtract the time for the first part. The last 55 km took the time that is left.

keyPoints.text: average speed for the whole journey was 80 km/h
keyPoints.note: Average speed = TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time. Use it to find the total time.
Change to hours: 1 h 30 min = 1.5 hours.

steps.explain: Distance of the first part: speed \(\times\) time, with 1 hour 30 minutes \(=1.5\) hours.
Total distance of the whole journey.
The average speed was 80 km/h, so the total time was distance \(\div\) speed.
The last part took the time left over after the first 1.5 hours.
Speed for the last part \(=\) distance \(\div\) time.
Check: \(55\text{ km}\) in half an hour is \(110\) km/h \(\checkmark\). Total: \(105+55=160\) km in \(1.5+0.5=2\) hours gives \(160\div2=80\) km/h. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Greg's weekly salary is \(\$70\) less than Joan's, whose weekly salary is \(\$50\) more than Sue's. If Sue earns \(\$280\) per week, how much in total do they earn per week?
questions.hint: Start with Sue (you know her pay), then find Joan, then Greg. The question asks for the TOTAL of all three weekly salaries.

keyPoints.note: Greg = Joan − 70 (not Sue − 70).
Add the salaries of Greg, Joan AND Sue.

steps.explain: Sue earns \(\$280\). Joan earns \(\$50\) more than Sue.
Greg earns \(\$70\) less than Joan.
Add the three weekly salaries.
Check: the option \(\$260\) is only Greg's salary. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem:
A small square patio required nine slabs to cover it.
The cost of using 4 patterned slabs and 5 plain ones is \(\$40\).
If 2 patterned slabs and 7 plain ones are used instead, the cost becomes \(\$38\).

Find the cost of this arrangement which is made up by using 8 patterned slabs and 1 plain one.

questions.stem: Alex finds that by wearing different combinations of the jackets, shirts and pairs of trousers that he owns, he can make up 90 different outfits. If he owns 5 jackets and 3 pairs of trousers, how many shirts does he own?
questions.hint: An outfit is ONE jacket AND ONE shirt AND ONE pair of trousers. The number of outfits is the product of the numbers of each item. Work backwards from 90.

keyPoints.note: Number of outfits = jackets × shirts × trousers.
Multiply these two first: 5 × 3.

steps.explain: Each outfit uses one jacket, one shirt and one pair of trousers, so multiply the numbers of choices. Let \(s\) be the number of shirts.
Multiply the known numbers: \(5\times3=15\).
Divide both sides by 15.
Check: \(5\times6\times3=90\) outfits. \(\checkmark\)

The price is for each lot of 500 sheets.

steps.explain: Change the height of the stack into centimetres.
Each sheet is 0.08 cm thick, so the number of sheets is:
Find how many lots of 500 sheets there are in 5000 sheets.
Each lot of 500 sheets costs \(\$3.00\).

questions.stem: If a kilogram is equal to approximately 2.2 pounds, which of the following is the best approximation of the number of kilograms in one pound?
questions.hint: One kilogram is MORE than one pound (2.2 pounds), so one pound must be LESS than one kilogram. Divide 1 by 2.2 and change the decimal to a fraction.

keyPoints.text: number of kilograms in one pound
keyPoints.note: One pound is less than 1 kg, so the answer must be a number less than 1, and this rules out 11/5.
1 kg = 2.2 lb, so 1 lb = 1 ÷ 2.2 kg.

steps.explain: 1 kg is 2.2 pounds, so 1 pound is \(1\div2.2\) kilograms.
Remove the decimal in the bottom by multiplying the top and bottom by 10.
Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by 2.
Check with decimals: \(\dfrac{5}{11}=0.4545\ldots\) and \(2.2\times0.4545=1\). \(\checkmark\) The option \(\dfrac{11}{5}=2.2\) is the number of POUNDS in a kilogram, the wrong way round.

questions.stem: The perimeter of a rectangle is 108 cm. The ratio of its length to its width is 7 : 2. What is the area of the rectangle in \(\text{cm}^2\) ?
questions.hint: The perimeter is 2 lengths + 2 widths, so length + width is HALF of 108. Share this between the length (7 parts) and the width (2 parts), then multiply to get the area.

keyPoints.text: The perimeter of a rectangle is 108 cm
keyPoints.note: Length + width = perimeter ÷ 2.

keyPoints.text: ratio of its length to its width is 7 : 2
keyPoints.note: Length is 7 parts and width is 2 parts: 9 parts together make length + width.

steps.explain: Half of the perimeter is the length plus the width.
The ratio \(7:2\) has \(7+2=9\) parts. Find one part.
Find the length and width.
Area \(=\) length \(\times\) width.
Check the perimeter: \(2(42+12)=2\times54=108\) cm. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Tony wants to cycle 12 km in one hour. He cycles the first 6 km at 10 km/h. How fast must he go in the rest of his journey?
questions.hint: Do NOT average the speeds. Find how long the first 6 km take, subtract from the 1 hour allowed, and then find the speed needed to cover the last 6 km in the time left.

keyPoints.note: He has exactly 60 minutes for the whole 12 km.
The rest is 12 − 6 = 6 km, and the time left is whatever remains of the hour.

steps.explain: Time for the first 6 km at 10 km/h: time \(=\) distance \(\div\) speed.
Time left from the one hour allowed.
The distance left is \(12-6=6\) km. The speed needed is distance \(\div\) time.
Check: the second half takes \(6\div15=0.4\) h \(=24\) min, and \(36+24=60\) minutes. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The sum of a denominator and a numerator is 84 and their difference is 14. What is the proper fraction in its simplest form?
questions.hint: A PROPER fraction has the numerator smaller than the denominator, so the difference is denominator \(-\) numerator. Use the sum and difference to find both numbers, then simplify.

keyPoints.note: A proper fraction has a smaller numerator than denominator.

keyPoints.text: sum of a denominator and a numerator is 84
keyPoints.note: d + n = 84. The difference is d − n = 14.

steps.explain: Let the denominator be \(d\) and the numerator \(n\). For a proper fraction \(d\) is bigger, so write the sum and the difference.
Add the two equations: the \(n\) terms cancel.
Find the numerator from the sum.
The fraction is \(\dfrac{35}{49}\). Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by 7.

questions.stem: The number 2002 is a palindromic number because it is unchanged if its digits are written in the reverse order. Which is the next palindromic year?
questions.hint: A palindromic 4-digit number reads the same backwards: its pattern is \(abba\). The year must come AFTER 2002. Keep the thousands digit 2 and try the smallest hundreds digit that makes a bigger number.

keyPoints.note: 'Next' means the first palindromic year AFTER 2002, so look for the smallest one that is bigger than 2002.

keyPoints.text: unchanged if its digits are written in the reverse order
keyPoints.note: The first digit equals the last digit, and the second digit equals the third digit.

steps.explain: A 4-digit palindrome has the form \(abba\): the thousands digit equals the units digit and the hundreds digit equals the tens digit. 2002 has \(a=2\), \(b=0\).
The next one must be bigger. Keep \(a=2\) and increase \(b\) to the next digit, 1: the number is 2112.
Check that nothing lies between: any palindrome starting with 2 and ending with 2 and with \(b=0\) is only 2002, so the next is 2112.
The other options: 1991 is before 2002, and 2552 and 3003 are palindromes but are later than 2112.

questions.stem: Jessica was given a box of chocolates that weighed 380 grams as a birthday present. She shared half of the chocolates with her friends. The remaining half box weighed 220 grams. She then ate the rest of the chocolates. What does the empty box weigh?
questions.hint: The weight lost when she shared HALF of the chocolates is the weight of that half of the chocolates. Use it to find the weight of all the chocolates, then take it away from 380 g to find the box.

keyPoints.note: The half she gave away weighs 380 − 220 grams.

keyPoints.text: What does the empty box weigh
keyPoints.note: Box = full weight − weight of ALL the chocolates.

steps.explain: After sharing, the weight fell from 380 g to 220 g. That lost weight is half of the chocolates.
All the chocolates weigh twice that.
The empty box is the full weight minus the weight of all the chocolates.
Check the half box: box \(60\) g + half the chocolates \(160\) g \(=220\) g. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: At a parade, balloons are given out in the order blue, red, red, yellow, yellow, yellow, blue, red, red, yellow, yellow, yellow, etc. If this pattern continues, how many red balloons will have been given out when a total of 70 balloons have been distributed?
questions.hint: Find the repeating block (blue, red, red, yellow, yellow, yellow): how many balloons are in it and how many are red? Divide 70 by the length of the block and look carefully at the remainder.

keyPoints.text: blue, red, red, yellow, yellow, yellow
keyPoints.note: This block of 6 balloons repeats: 1 blue, 2 red, 3 yellow.
70 may not be an exact multiple of the block length: check the leftover balloons.

steps.explain: The pattern repeats every 6 balloons: blue, red, red, yellow, yellow, yellow. Each block has 2 red balloons.
Divide 70 by 6 to find the number of complete blocks and the leftover balloons.
11 complete blocks give 11 lots of 2 red balloons.
The 4 leftover balloons are the start of the next block: blue, red, red, yellow. They include 2 red balloons.
Add the red balloons.
Check: in 70 balloons, \(66\) are in complete blocks and \(4\) are left. The option 22 forgets the red balloons in the leftover part. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Four European teams enter a football tournament. Each team plays one match against each of the other teams, with three points for a win, one point for a draw and none for a defeat. Which team wins?
options: one win, one tie, one loss
one win, zero tie, two loss
no wins, two ties, one loss
one win, two ties, no loss
questions.hint: Each team plays 3 matches (one against each of the other three teams). Work out the total points of each team using 3 points for a win, 1 for a draw and 0 for a loss. The team with the most points wins.

keyPoints.text: three points for a win, one point for a draw and none for a defeat
keyPoints.note: Points = 3 × wins + 1 × draws (a tie is a draw).
The winner is the team with the MOST points, not the most wins.

steps.explain: Each team plays the other 3 teams, so every option has 3 matches (wins + ties + losses = 3). Work out the points for each option.
Option A: one win, one tie, one loss.
Option B: one win, no ties, two losses.
Option C: no wins, two ties, one loss.
Option D: one win, two ties, no losses.
Compare: 4, 3, 2 and 5 points. Option D has the most points, so that team wins. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: There are 555 students in a school. How many desks does the school need if two children sit at each desk?
questions.hint: Divide the number of students by 2. If there is a remainder, the last student still needs a desk, so round UP.

keyPoints.text: two children sit at each desk
keyPoints.note: Divide 555 by 2.

keyPoints.text: How many desks does the school need
keyPoints.note: Desks come whole. A leftover student still needs a desk, so round up.

steps.explain: Divide the number of students by 2.
277 desks seat \(277\times2=554\) students. One student is left without a desk.
So one more desk is needed for the last student.
Check: 278 desks seat up to \(278\times2=556\) students, which is enough for 555. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: What is the angle between the hour hand and the minute hand at 2:20pm on an analogue clock?
questions.hint: A full turn of the clock is \(360^\circ\). The minute hand turns \(6^\circ\) per minute. The hour hand turns \(30^\circ\) per hour AND creeps forward as the minutes pass (\(0.5^\circ\) per minute). Find where each hand points (measured from 12) and subtract.

keyPoints.note: At 2:20 the hour hand has moved past the 2, one third of the way to the 3.

keyPoints.text: angle between the hour hand and the minute hand
keyPoints.note: Find the position of each hand in degrees from 12, then subtract.

questions.stem: A 100-litre vessel is full of a mixture of orange juice concentrate and water, in which there is 30% concentrate. 50 litres are sold, and the vessel is filled up with water. What is the new percentage of the juice concentration now?
questions.hint: Find the litres of concentrate in the vessel. The mixture is the same everywhere, so when half of it is sold, half of the concentrate goes too. Then work out the percentage of concentrate in the new 100 litres.

keyPoints.note: The mixture is evenly mixed, so half the vessel is sold and half the concentrate goes with it.
The vessel is back to 100 litres, but the extra 50 litres is only water.

steps.explain: Find the amount of concentrate at the start: 30% of 100 litres.
50 litres (half) of the mixture is sold, so half of the concentrate is sold too. The vessel keeps half of the concentrate.
The vessel is filled up to 100 litres with water. Water adds no concentrate, so there are still 15 litres of concentrate in 100 litres.
Change to a percentage.
Check: topping up with water (50 L of pure water added to 50 L of 30% mixture) halves the strength: \(30\%\div2=15\%\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A girl rides her bike 5 km in 15 minutes. How long will it take her to ride 43 km, assuming she doesn't get tired?
questions.hint: Find how long she takes for 1 km (15 minutes \(\div5\)), then multiply by 43. Change the minutes to hours and minutes. Watch the units in the options.

keyPoints.note: Every 5 km takes 15 minutes, so each km takes 3 minutes.
Multiply the time for 1 km by 43.

steps.explain: Find the time for 1 km.
Multiply by 43 km.
Change 129 minutes to hours and minutes: 60 minutes is 1 hour, so 120 minutes is 2 hours.
So the ride takes 2 hours 9 minutes. The option “129 hours” uses the wrong unit.
Check: in 2 hours 9 minutes she rides at 20 km/h for 2.15 hours: \(20\times2.15=43\) km. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Which of the following shapes has 3 axes of symmetry?
questions.hint: An axis of symmetry is a line that folds the shape exactly onto itself. Count the axes for each shape: think about folding along lines through the corners and along lines through the middle of the sides.

keyPoints.note: Count the fold lines of each shape. Only one of the four shapes has exactly 3.

steps.explain: Square: it has 4 axes of symmetry (2 diagonals, 1 horizontal and 1 vertical line through the middle).
Rhombus (that is not a square): the only axes are the 2 diagonals.
Circle: any line through the centre is an axis of symmetry, so it has infinitely many.
Equilateral triangle: each axis goes from a corner to the middle of the opposite side. There are 3 corners, so 3 axes.

questions.hint: A fraction bar means DIVIDE. So \(\dfrac{12}{\frac14}\) means \(12\div\dfrac14\). Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal (flip it). Or ask: how many quarters are in 12?

keyPoints.note: The big fraction bar means 12 ÷ 1/4: how many quarters fit into 12?

steps.explain: The fraction bar means division: 12 divided by one quarter.
Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal. The reciprocal of \(\dfrac14\) is \(\dfrac41=4\).
Calculate.
Check with meaning: each whole has 4 quarters, so 12 wholes contain \(12\times4=48\) quarters. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: What is the sum of two consecutive even numbers, if the difference of the squares is 84?
questions.hint: Call the two numbers \(n\) and \(n+2\) (consecutive even numbers differ by 2). Use the difference of two squares: \(a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)\). The sum \(a+b\) is what you want!

keyPoints.note: They differ by exactly 2: n and n + 2.

keyPoints.text: the difference of the squares is 84
keyPoints.note: (n + 2)² − n² = 84. Use the factorisation (a − b)(a + b).

steps.explain: Let the two consecutive even numbers be \(a\) (larger) and \(b\) (smaller), with \(a-b=2\). The difference of the squares is:
Factorise the difference of two squares: \(a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b)\).
Replace \(a-b\) by 2.
Divide by 2. The sum \(a+b\) is exactly what the question asks for.
Check by finding the numbers: \(a+b=42\) and \(a-b=2\) give \(a=22\) and \(b=20\). Then \(22^2-20^2=484-400=84\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: How many \(\dfrac23\) cup sugar bowls can be filled from 18 cups of sugar?
questions.hint: This is a division question: how many lots of \(\dfrac23\) fit into 18? Divide 18 by \(\dfrac23\) (multiply by the reciprocal). Think: each cup fills 1\(\frac12\) bowls, so 18 cups should fill more than 18 bowls.

keyPoints.note: Each bowl holds 2/3 of a cup. Count how many bowls 18 cups can fill: 18 ÷ 2/3.

steps.explain: We want to know how many lots of \(\dfrac23\) cup are in 18 cups, so divide.
Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal. The reciprocal of \(\dfrac23\) is \(\dfrac32\).
Calculate: \(18\div2=9\), then \(9\times3=27\).
Check: 27 bowls of \(\dfrac23\) cup use \(27\times\dfrac23=18\) cups. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Subtract from the difference of 202 and 2 the product of 13.9 and 9.
questions.hint: Translate the words into a calculation. “The difference of 202 and 2” is \(202-2\). “The product of 13.9 and 9” is \(13.9\times9\). “Subtract A from B” means \(B-A\).

keyPoints.text: Subtract from the difference of 202 and 2 the product of 13.9 and 9
keyPoints.note: Take the product AWAY FROM the difference: (202 − 2) − (13.9 × 9).

steps.explain: Work out “the difference of 202 and 2”.
Work out “the product of 13.9 and 9”: \(13\times9=117\) and \(0.9\times9=8.1\).
Subtract the product FROM the difference (the second quantity is taken away from the first).
Subtract.

questions.stem: The sum of five consecutive integers is 510. What is the average of these five numbers?
questions.hint: The average of a list is the sum divided by how many numbers there are. You already know both.

keyPoints.text: The sum of five consecutive integers is 510
keyPoints.note: The sum is 510 and there are 5 numbers.
Average = sum ÷ number of values.

steps.explain: The average is the total divided by the number of values. There are 5 numbers.
Substitute the sum 510.
Check: five consecutive integers with the average 102 in the middle are 100, 101, 102, 103, 104. Their sum is \(100+101+102+103+104=510\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: If the average of 3 and x is 5, and the average of 5 and y is 7, what is the average of x and y?
questions.hint: Use each average to find the missing number: average of two numbers \(=\) (their sum) \(\div2\), so the sum is double the average. Find \(x\) and \(y\), then average them.

keyPoints.text: the average of 3 and x is 5
the average of 5 and y is 7

steps.explain: The average of 3 and \(x\) is 5, so their sum is 10.
The average of 5 and \(y\) is 7, so their sum is 14.
Now find the average of \(x\) and \(y\).
Check: \(\dfrac{3+7}{2}=5\) \(\checkmark\) and \(\dfrac{5+9}{2}=7\) \(\checkmark\).

questions.stem: What is the surface area of one cube if two identical cubes stuck together have a volume of 1458 units?
questions.hint: Two identical cubes together have a volume of 1458, so one cube has half of that volume. Find the side of the cube (the number that multiplies by itself three times). A cube has 6 faces of side \(\times\) side.

keyPoints.text: two identical cubes stuck together have a volume of 1458
keyPoints.note: One cube has half this volume.
Surface area = 6 × (side × side).

steps.explain: The volume of one cube is half of the combined volume.
Find the side: the number that multiplies by itself 3 times to give 729. Try 9: \(9\times9=81\) and \(81\times9=729\).
A cube has 6 identical square faces. Find the area of one face.
Surface area \(=6\times\) area of one face.
Check: the options 729 and 81 are the volume and one face. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: If the product of two integers is odd, which of the following must be true?
options: The difference between the two integers is an odd number.
The sum of the squares of the two integers is an odd number.
The difference between the squares of the two integers is an odd number.
The square of either integer is an odd number.
questions.hint: A product is odd only when BOTH numbers are odd (if one number is even, the product is even). So both integers are odd. Then test each statement with two odd numbers such as 3 and 5.

keyPoints.text: product of two integers is odd
keyPoints.note: Odd × odd = odd, but even × anything = even. So BOTH integers must be odd.
It must be true for every pair of odd integers.

steps.explain: If either integer were even, the product would be even. So the product is odd only when BOTH integers are odd.
Test statement A with 3 and 5: the difference of two odd numbers is even.
Test statement B: odd squared is odd, and odd plus odd is even.
Test statement C: odd minus odd is even.
Statement D: the square of an odd number is odd times odd, which is odd. This holds for each of the two integers.
So only statement D must be true.

questions.hint: Each square is attached at the MIDPOINT of the side of the square to its right, so each square has half the side of the one before it. Find the three side lengths, then the perimeter of the staircase shape. (Tip: for a staircase made of right angles, slide the horizontal edges and vertical edges to make a rectangle.)

keyPoints.text: attached at the mid point of the side
keyPoints.note: The next square starts at the middle of the side, so its side is half as long as the side before it.
Perimeter = total length around the outside of the whole shape.

steps.explain: The largest square has side 6. The next square is attached at the midpoint of its right side, so its side is half of 6. The third square is half of that.

How many times larger is the area of the largest square than that of the smallest square?

</svg>

questions.hint: First compare the SIDES of the largest and smallest squares. An area is side \(\times\) side, so the area ratio is the side ratio multiplied by itself.

keyPoints.text: How many times larger is the area
keyPoints.note: Compare AREAS, not sides. If the sides are 4 times as long, the area is 4 × 4 times as big.

steps.explain: Each square has half the side of the previous one, so the sides are 6, 3 and 1.5.

questions.hint: Work with fractions of the whole field. After day 1 find the REMAINDER (a fraction of the whole). The next day he covers two fifths OF THAT REMAINDER. Add up the first two days, then the last day is what remains.

keyPoints.note: Two fifths of what was LEFT after day 1, not two fifths of the whole field.
The last day covers whatever is left after the first two days.

questions.stem: A teacher wants to make a test containing 20 verbal and 30 math questions. Each verbal question is to be allotted 45 seconds to complete and each math question is to be given a certain amount of time. If the whole test is for 55 minutes, how long should she allow for each maths question?
questions.hint: Change everything into the same unit (seconds). Find the time for all the verbal questions, take it away from the 55-minute total, and share what is left between the 30 maths questions.

keyPoints.note: Verbal questions are measured in seconds but the test is in minutes. Change to one unit.

keyPoints.text: how long should she allow for each maths question
keyPoints.note: Maths time ÷ 30 = time for one question.

steps.explain: Time for the 20 verbal questions at 45 seconds each.
Time left for the maths questions out of the 55 minutes.
Share this time between the 30 maths questions.
Change 80 seconds to minutes and seconds: 60 seconds is 1 minute, so 80 seconds is 1 minute 20 seconds.
Check: \(20\times45+30\times80=900+2400=3300\) seconds, and \(3300\div60=55\) minutes. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem:
The diagram shows 4 identical shaded triangles in a rectangle.

The rectangle measures 36 centimetres by 24 centimetres. Calculate the area of one shaded triangle.

questions.stem: In a survey, the ratio of the number of people who preferred milk chocolate to those who preferred plain chocolate was 5 : 3. If 80 more people preferred milk chocolate to plain chocolate, how many people preferred plain chocolate?
questions.hint: In the ratio 5 : 3, milk has 5 parts and plain has 3 parts. The DIFFERENCE between the parts is \(5-3=2\) parts, and this equals 80 people. Find one part, then the plain chocolate people.

keyPoints.note: 80 is the DIFFERENCE between the two groups: 5 parts − 3 parts.

keyPoints.text: how many people preferred plain chocolate
keyPoints.note: The answer is 3 parts, not 5.

steps.explain: Milk chocolate is 5 parts and plain chocolate is 3 parts. The difference is:
This difference is 80 people, so find one part.
Plain chocolate is 3 parts.
Check: milk chocolate is \(5\times40=200\), and \(200-120=80\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The total fare for 2 adults and 3 children on an excursion boat is \(\$14.00\). If each child's fare is one half of each adult's fare, what is the adult fare?
questions.hint: Write the children's fare in terms of the adult fare: a child pays half an adult fare. Then count the total in “adult fares” (3 children are one and a half adults).

keyPoints.text: each child's fare is one half of each adult's fare
keyPoints.note: Child fare = ½ × adult fare. Convert the children into adult fares.
Answer is the fare of ONE adult.

steps.explain: Let one adult fare be \(a\). A child pays half of that, \(\dfrac{a}{2}\).
3 children pay \(3\times\dfrac{a}{2}=1.5a\). Add the 2 adults.
The total fare is \(\$14.00\).
Divide both sides by 3.5.
Check: a child pays \(\$2\). Then \(2\times4+3\times2=8+6=\$14\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Bob finishes the first half of an exam in two-thirds the time it takes him to finish the second half. If the whole exam takes him an hour, how many minutes does he spend on the first half of the exam?
questions.hint: If the first half takes \(\dfrac23\) of the time of the second half, the times are in the ratio 2 : 3. Change 1 hour to minutes and share it in that ratio.

keyPoints.text: two-thirds the time it takes him to finish the second half
keyPoints.note: first half : second half = 2 : 3.
1 hour = 60 minutes.

steps.explain: The first half takes \(\dfrac23\) of the time of the second half, so the times are in the ratio 2 : 3.
The whole exam takes 60 minutes and the ratio has \(2+3=5\) parts.
The first half is 2 parts.
Check: the second half takes \(3\times12=36\) minutes and \(\dfrac23\times36=24\). \(\checkmark\) Total \(24+36=60\) minutes.

questions.stem: Joseph bought a house for \(\$80,000\). If he sells it for a profit of 12.5 percent of the original cost, what is the selling price of the house?
questions.hint: The profit is 12.5% OF THE ORIGINAL COST (\(\$80,000\)). The selling price is the cost PLUS the profit. Remember 12.5% is one eighth.

keyPoints.text: a profit of 12.5 percent of the original cost
keyPoints.note: Profit = 12.5% of \(\$80,000\). Then ADD it to the cost.
Selling price = cost + profit, not just the profit.

steps.explain: Find the profit: 12.5% is the same as one eighth.
The selling price is the original cost plus the profit.
Check with a decimal: the selling price is 112.5% of the cost, \(80\,000\times1.125=90\,000\). \(\checkmark\) The option \(\$10,000\) is only the profit.

questions.stem: If 65 percent of x is 195, what is 75 percent of x?
questions.hint: First find \(x\) (the whole). 65% of \(x\) is 195, so divide 195 by 0.65. Then find 75% of \(x\). A shortcut: find what 5% is worth.

keyPoints.note: x is the WHOLE (100%). 195 is only 65% of it.
Once you have x, find 75% of it.

steps.explain: Write the first sentence as an equation.
Divide both sides by 0.65.
Now find 75% of 300.
Check with a shortcut: 5% of \(x\) is \(300\times0.05=15\), and 75% is 10 more than 65%, which is \(2\times15=30\) more: \(195+30=225\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A painter charges \(\$12\) an hour while his son charges \(\$6\) an hour. If father and son work the same amount of time together on a job, how many hours does each of them work if their combined charge for labour is \(\$108\)?
questions.hint: Find how much the father and son charge TOGETHER for each hour of work, then divide the total charge by that amount.

keyPoints.text: work the same amount of time together
keyPoints.note: Both work the same number of hours, so in each hour they earn 12 + 6 dollars.
Total charge = (combined hourly rate) × hours.

steps.explain: Each hour of the job the two together charge:
The total is \(\$108\), so the number of hours is the total divided by the combined hourly charge.
Check: in 6 hours the father charges \(6\times12=\$72\) and the son charges \(6\times6=\$36\). \(72+36=\$108\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: If a divisor is 23, the quotient is 5 and the remainder is 2, what is the number you are dividing?
questions.hint: Division with a remainder follows the rule: number \(=\) divisor \(\times\) quotient \(+\) remainder. Do not forget to add the remainder.

keyPoints.text: divisor is 23, the quotient is 5 and the remainder is 2
keyPoints.note: number = 23 × 5 + 2. The remainder is added at the end.

steps.explain: The number being divided (the dividend) equals the divisor times the quotient, plus the remainder.
Substitute the values.
Multiply first, then add: \(23\times5=115\).
Check by dividing: \(117\div23=5\) remainder 2 (\(23\times5=115\) and \(117-115=2\)). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The product of two numbers is 1875 and the quotient, when the larger one is divided by the smaller, is 3. The sum of the numbers is:
questions.hint: If the larger number divided by the smaller is 3, the larger number is 3 times the smaller. Call the smaller number \(s\); then the product is \(s\times3s\). Find \(s\).

keyPoints.text: the quotient, when the larger one is divided by the smaller, is 3
keyPoints.note: larger = 3 × smaller.
The question asks for smaller + larger.

steps.explain: Let the smaller number be \(s\). The larger number is 3 times the smaller, so it is \(3s\).
The product of the two numbers is 1875.
Divide by 3, then find the number that multiplies by itself to give 625.
The larger number is 3 times 25.
The sum of the numbers:
Check: \(25\times75=1875\) \(\checkmark\) and \(75\div25=3\) \(\checkmark\).

questions.stem: Express 4 tens, 51 tenths and 9 thousandths as a decimal.
questions.hint: Turn each part into a number first. 4 tens is 40. 51 tenths is 51 lots of 0.1 (watch out: 51 tenths is MORE than 5!). 9 thousandths is 0.009. Then add.

keyPoints.note: 9 thousandths = 0.009 (three decimal places).

steps.explain: 4 tens means 4 groups of ten.
51 tenths means 51 lots of \(\dfrac1{10}\), which is \(51\div10\).
9 thousandths is 9 lots of \(\dfrac{1}{1000}\).
Check the place values: 4 tens, 5 ones, 1 tenth, 0 hundredths, 9 thousandths gives 45.109. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A glass holds 180 mL of juice when it is one quarter empty. How much does it hold when it is one quarter full?
questions.hint: “One quarter empty” is NOT the same as “one quarter full”. If a quarter is empty, how much of the glass is full? Use that to find one quarter of the glass.

keyPoints.note: If one quarter is empty, then three quarters are full.
Find one quarter of the glass: the answer is smaller than 180 mL.

steps.explain: When the glass is one quarter empty, three quarters of it is full.
The 180 mL is three quarters of the glass. Find one quarter by dividing by 3.
When the glass is one quarter full, it holds one quarter of the glass.
Check: the full glass holds \(4\times60=240\) mL and three quarters of 240 is \(180\) mL. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: There are 5 coins in the first pile, 8 in the second, 11 in the third, and 16 in the fourth. What is the least number of coins that I have to move to make these four piles have the same number of coins?
questions.hint: Find the total number of coins and share it equally to find how many each pile should have (the average). The coins that must be moved are the EXTRA coins in the piles that are above the average.

keyPoints.note: Each pile must end with the average number of coins.

keyPoints.text: least number of coins that I have to move
keyPoints.note: Only move coins OUT of piles that have too many; count each coin moved once.

steps.explain: Find the total number of coins.
Share equally between the 4 piles.
Piles with more than 10 coins have extra coins that must be moved: the third pile has 1 extra and the fourth pile has 6 extra.

The extras are the coins that have to move: 1 from the third pile and 6 from the fourth pile. These are exactly the coins the two small piles are missing (the first pile needs 5 more and the second pile needs 2 more, which is also 7).

Check by moving the coins: put 5 coins on the first pile and 2 coins on the second pile, taking them from the third (1 coin) and fourth (6 coins) piles. The piles become 10, 10, 10, 10. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: On a trip, there are 9 children and 2 adults per boat. If a total of 99 people went on this boat trip, how many were children?
questions.hint: Find how many people are in ONE boat, then how many boats are needed for 99 people. The number of children is the number of boats times 9 (not the number of boats!).

keyPoints.note: Each boat carries 9 + 2 = 11 people.
The question asks for the number of CHILDREN, not boats and not people.

steps.explain: People in each boat.
Number of boats for 99 people.
Each boat has 9 children.
Check: the adults are \(9\times2=18\), and \(81+18=99\). \(\checkmark\) The option 11 is the number of people per boat.

Check: the area does not depend on \(\pi\) at all, which makes sense because the semicircles cancel. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Which statement is true?
options: Multiplying a number by 1.25 is the same as dividing by 0.75
Multiplying a number by 1.20 is the same as dividing by 0.80
Multiplying a number by 1.25 is the same as dividing by 0.80
Multiplying a number by 1.20 is the same as dividing by 0.75
questions.hint: Dividing by a number is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal (one divided by the number). Work out \(1\div0.75\) and \(1\div0.80\) and compare with 1.25 and 1.20.

keyPoints.note: Only one statement is correct. Convert each “dividing by” into “multiplying by”.

steps.explain: Dividing by 0.80 is the same as multiplying by \(1\div0.80\). Write 0.80 as the fraction \(\dfrac45\); its reciprocal is \(\dfrac54\).
So dividing by 0.80 is the same as multiplying by 1.25. This matches statement C.
Check the others. Dividing by 0.75 is multiplying by \(\dfrac43=1.333\ldots\), which is not 1.25 or 1.20, so statements A and D are false.
Statement B says that multiplying by 1.20 equals dividing by 0.80, but dividing by 0.80 is multiplying by 1.25, not 1.20.
Test with the number 100: \(100\times1.25=125\) and \(100\div0.8=125\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: 5 thousands + 20 hundreds + 41 tens + 2 units =
questions.hint: Change each part into a number first: 5 thousands is \(5\times1000\), 20 hundreds is \(20\times100\), 41 tens is \(41\times10\). Then add all four parts.

keyPoints.note: 20 hundreds = 20 × 100 = 2000 (more than 9 of a place value is allowed here).

steps.explain: Write the value of each part.
41 tens means 41 groups of 10, and 2 units is just 2.
Add the four parts, taking the largest ones first: \(5000+2000=7000\).
Add the units.
Check the options: 5242 forgets that 20 hundreds is 2000 and 41 tens is 410. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Which of the following fractions is closest in value to the decimal 0.04?
questions.hint: Change each fraction into a decimal (divide the top by the bottom). Then find how far each decimal is from 0.04. The smallest distance wins. Remember 0.04 is a very small number.

keyPoints.text: closest in value to the decimal 0.04
keyPoints.note: 'Closest' means the smallest DIFFERENCE from 0.04. Subtract each decimal from the number or vice versa.

steps.explain: Change each fraction into a decimal.
Find how far each decimal is from 0.04 (subtract 0.04 from each).
Continue with the other two.
The smallest difference is 0.293, which belongs to \(\dfrac13\). Since 0.04 is smaller than every fraction here, the smallest fraction is the closest.
So \(\dfrac13\) is the closest in value to 0.04.

questions.stem: Different four-letter passwords can be constructed using the letters A, B, C and D only once. How many such passwords exist if either C or B must be in the second position?
questions.hint: Split the problem into two cases: C in the second position, and B in the second position. For each case, count how many ways the other three letters can fill the remaining three places (3 choices, then 2, then 1).

keyPoints.note: Each letter is used exactly once in each password.

keyPoints.text: either C or B must be in the second position
keyPoints.note: Two separate cases: C second, or B second. Add the cases.

steps.explain: Case 1: C is in the second position. The other three letters A, B and D fill the other three places, in any order. There are 3 choices for the first place, 2 for the next, and 1 for the last.
Case 2: B is in the second position. The same count applies for A, C and D in the other three places.
The cases cannot both happen at once (only one letter can be in the second position), so add them.
Check: all passwords with any of the 4 letters second would be \(4\times6=24\); C or B second is half of them (2 of the 4 letters), so \(24\div2=12\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A runner began a marathon at 2.35 pm. It took him 3 hours and 45 minutes to run the race. He crossed the finish line at
questions.hint: Add the hours first, then the minutes. When the minutes pass 60, carry 1 hour. Remember that 60 minutes make an hour (not 100).

keyPoints.note: Start time is 2:35 in the afternoon, so the finish is also pm.
Add 3 hours first, then add the 45 minutes.

steps.explain: Add the 3 hours to the start time of 2.35 pm.
Add the 45 minutes. \(35+45=80\) minutes, which is 1 hour 20 minutes. So the hour goes up by 1 and the minutes become 20.
The runner finished at 6.20 pm (it is still the afternoon, so not am).

Check by subtracting: from 2.35 pm to 6.35 pm is 4 hours, which is 15 minutes too many (because \(4\text{ h}-3\text{ h }45\text{ min}=15\text{ min}\)), so the finish is 6.35 pm \(-\) 15 min \(=\) 6.20 pm. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: If the 13th of November 2008 was on a Thursday, on what day was 25th December 2008?
questions.hint: Count the number of days from 13 November to 25 December (November has 30 days). Then divide by 7: the remainder tells you how many days the weekday moves forward.

keyPoints.text: 13th of November 2008 was on a Thursday
keyPoints.note: Start counting from a Thursday and use groups of 7 days.
Count the days between the two dates, remembering November has 30 days.

steps.explain: Days left in November after the 13th: from 13 to 30 November.
Then 25 more days of December to reach the 25th.
A week has 7 days, so divide 42 by 7.
After exactly 6 weeks it is the same day of the week as the start.
Check: 13 Nov, 20 Nov, 27 Nov, 4 Dec, 11 Dec, 18 Dec, 25 Dec are all Thursdays (7 days apart). \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: A football team has won 10 games and lost 5 games. If the team wins the remaining games of the season, it will have won 80 percent of its games. How many games in total will have been played?
questions.hint: If the team wins ALL the remaining games, it will lose no more games, so the 5 games already lost are the only losses. These 5 losses will be the other 20 percent of all the games.

keyPoints.note: From now on only wins are added, so the number of losses stays at 5.
If 80% are wins, then 20% are losses.

steps.explain: After winning all the remaining games the team has won 80% of its games, so it has lost the other part.
The team has lost 5 games and will lose no more, so 5 games are 20% of the season.
Find 100% by multiplying by 5.
Check: 25 games, 5 lost, so 20 won. \(20\div25=0.8=80\%\). Also the team has already won 10 and will win \(20-10=10\) more of the remaining 10 games (25 \(-\) 15). \(\checkmark\)

keyPoints.text: X is halfway between Q and R

questions.hint: The diagonals of a rectangle cross at the middle of the rectangle, which is also the midpoint of each diagonal. Find the midpoint of the diagonal from P to R (average the x's and average the y's).

keyPoints.note: The diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other, so they meet at the midpoint of the rectangle.

steps.explain: The diagonals of a rectangle cross at their midpoints. Use the diagonal from P \((2,4)\) to R \((6,2)\).

questions.hint: The big square is made of the shaded square AND four identical right triangles in the corners. Find the side of the big square from the two labelled lengths, then the area of the four triangles, and take them away from the whole.

keyPoints.note: Congruent means all four triangles are exactly the same, so find the area of one and multiply by 4.

keyPoints.text: fraction of the shaded part as a fraction of the whole figure
keyPoints.note: Fraction = shaded area ÷ area of the whole big square.

steps.explain: Along the top edge the corner triangle takes 10 cm, and along the right edge the triangle takes 30 cm. Each side of the big square is made of a short side (10 cm) and a long side (30 cm) of the triangles.

questions.stem: Which type of graph would you use to show the number of pages in each book in the classroom library?
questions.hint: Think about the data: it is a long list of NUMBERS (pages in each book) that can be large, one number for each book. Which graph can show every single number and also show how the numbers are spread?

keyPoints.text: the number of pages in each book
keyPoints.note: There is one number for each book, so there are many different values. Choose the graph that shows every value.

steps.explain: The data is a list of many different numbers (for example 24, 37, 41, 56, 58, ...), one for each book.

A pictograph uses symbols that stand for several items, so it suits small counts of categories, not a long list of page numbers. A sector graph shows parts of a whole (percentages), and a double bar graph compares two sets of categories.
A stem-and-leaf plot writes down every value by splitting each number into a stem (tens) and a leaf (units) and shows the spread of all the values at once.
So the stem-and-leaf plot is the best choice.

questions.stem: \(\$7.32\) is 15% of what amount?
questions.hint: \(\$7.32\) is only a PART (15%) of the whole amount, so the whole must be bigger than \(\$7.32\). Write 15% as 0.15 and divide.

keyPoints.note: The unknown amount is the WHOLE (100%). Divide the part by 0.15.

steps.explain: Call the whole amount \(A\). 15% of \(A\) is \(\$7.32\).
Divide both sides by 0.15.
Multiply the top and bottom by 100 to remove the decimal points: \(732\div15\). Then divide: \(15\times48=720\), remainder 12, and \(12\div15=0.8\).

questions.stem: How many odd integers are between \(\dfrac{10}{3}\) and \(\dfrac{62}{3}\)?
questions.hint: Change both fractions into mixed numbers or decimals to see the range, then list the odd whole numbers that lie strictly between them.

keyPoints.note: Convert the improper fractions to decimals: 10 ÷ 3 and 62 ÷ 3.
Odd whole numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7, ...

steps.explain: Change the fractions into mixed numbers: \(10\div3=3\) remainder 1, and \(62\div3=20\) remainder 2.
The odd integers between \(3\dfrac13\) and \(20\dfrac23\) start at 5 (3 is too small) and end at 19 (21 is too big).
Count them.
Check with a formula: the odd numbers from 5 to 19 go up by 2, so the count is \((19-5)\div2+1=7+1=8\). \(\checkmark\)
