questions.stem: What is the greatest integer that will divide evenly into both 36 and 54?
questions.hint: This asks for the highest common factor (HCF) of 36 and 54. List the factors of each number, or use prime factors, and pick the biggest one they share.

keyPoints.text: greatest integer that will divide evenly into both
keyPoints.note: That is the highest common factor (HCF): the largest number that is a factor of both numbers.

steps.explain: List the factors of 36 (the whole numbers that divide it exactly).
List the factors of 54.
Find the factors that appear in both lists: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. The biggest is 18.
Check with prime factors: \(36=2^2\times3^2\) and \(54=2\times3^3\). Take the smallest power of each prime: \(2\times3^2=18\).

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: If the sum of three different prime numbers is an even number, what is the smallest of the three?
options: It cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.hint: Think about odd and even. Every prime number except one is odd. What happens when you add three odd numbers? Which prime must be included to make the sum even?

keyPoints.text: sum of three different prime numbers is an even number
keyPoints.note: Odd + odd + odd = odd, so the three primes cannot all be odd.
Once you know which prime must be in the list, decide whether it is the smallest.

steps.explain: The only even prime number is 2. All other prime numbers (3, 5, 7, 11, ...) are odd.
If all three primes were odd, their sum would be odd (odd + odd = even, then even + odd = odd), but the sum is even. So one of the three primes must be the even prime, 2.
With 2 in the list, the sum is even + odd + odd = even. For example \(2+3+5=10\) or \(2+5+7=14\).
2 is smaller than every other prime, so it is the smallest of the three.

questions.stem: For how many positive integers x is \(\dfrac{130}{x}\) a whole number?
questions.hint: \(\dfrac{130}{x}\) is a whole number exactly when \(x\) divides 130 evenly. So count the positive factors of 130. Use factor pairs so you do not miss any.

keyPoints.note: x must be a factor of 130. Count ALL its factors, including 1 and 130.

steps.explain: For \(\dfrac{130}{x}\) to be a whole number, \(x\) must divide 130 exactly. List the factor pairs of 130 (two numbers that multiply to 130).
Each pair gives two different factors. Write all the factors in order.
Count the factors.
Check with prime factors: \(130=2\times5\times13\), three different primes, each used once. The number of factors is \(2\times2\times2=8\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: In the repeating decimal \(0.097531097531\ldots\), what is the 44th digit to the right of the decimal point?
questions.hint: Find the block of digits that repeats (here the digits 0, 9, 7, 5, 3, 1). Divide 44 by the length of the block: the REMAINDER tells you which digit of the block is the 44th digit.

keyPoints.note: The same block of digits repeats forever.
Divide 44 by the length of the block and use the remainder.

steps.explain: The repeating block is 097531, which has 6 digits: 0, 9, 7, 5, 3, 1.
Divide 44 by 6 to see how many complete blocks fit and what is left over.
7 complete blocks use the first 42 digits. The 44th digit is the 2nd digit of the next block.
The 2nd digit of the block 0, 9, 7, 5, 3, 1 is 9.
Check: the digits at positions 2, 8, 14, ..., 44 (every 6th digit from the 2nd) are all 9. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The sum of three consecutive integers is 312. What is the sum of the next three consecutive integers?
questions.hint: Each of the next three integers is exactly 3 more than the matching integer in the first group. So the sum goes up by \(3\times3\). Or find the numbers: the middle one is the average.

keyPoints.note: The next group starts right after the first group: every number is 3 bigger than its partner.

steps.explain: For three consecutive integers the middle number is the average of the three: \(312\div3=104\). So they are 103, 104 and 105.
The next three consecutive integers are 106, 107 and 108.
Add them.
Check with the shortcut: each of the three numbers went up by 3, so the sum goes up by \(3\times3=9\). \(312+9=321\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: What is 35% of a number if 12 is 15% of the same number?
questions.hint: First use 15% to find the whole number (100%). Then find 35% of it. A shortcut: 15% = 12, so 5% = 4.

keyPoints.note: 12 is only 15% of the number, so the number is bigger than 12.
Find 35% of the number you found, not of 12.

steps.explain: 15% of the number is 12. Find 5% by dividing by 3.
35% is 7 lots of 5%.
Check by finding the number: 100% is 20 lots of 5%, so \(20\times4=80\). Then \(35\%\text{ of }80=0.35\times80=28\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A man earns N dollars a month and spends S dollars a month on rent. If he then spends \(\dfrac38\) of the remainder on food, how much, in dollars, is left over for other expenses, in terms of N and S?
questions.hint: Work in steps. First find the REMAINDER after the rent. Then he spends \(\dfrac38\) of that remainder on food, so \(\dfrac58\) of the remainder is left.

keyPoints.text: spends S dollars a month on rent
keyPoints.note: After rent, the money left is N − S (subtract, not add).
If 3/8 of the remainder goes on food, then 1 − 3/8 = 5/8 of the remainder is left.

steps.explain: After paying rent \(S\) from his earnings \(N\), the remainder is:
He spends \(\dfrac38\) of this remainder on food. The fraction of the remainder that is left is:
So the money left over for other expenses is \(\dfrac58\) of the remainder.
Check with numbers: let \(N=1000\) and \(S=200\). The remainder is 800, food is \(\dfrac38\times800=300\), so \(800-300=500\). The formula gives \(\dfrac58\times800=500\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Michael travelled \(\dfrac25\) of his journey at 50 km/h. The next \(\dfrac15\) of his journey he travelled at 40 km/h. The remaining 40 km he covered in half an hour. How much time did he take for the whole journey?
questions.hint: Find what fraction of the journey is the remaining 40 km, and use it to find the whole journey in km. Then work out the time of each part (time \(=\) distance \(\div\) speed) and add the three times.

keyPoints.note: The remaining part is 1 − 2/5 − 1/5 of the journey, and it is 40 km.

keyPoints.text: How much time did he take for the whole journey
keyPoints.note: Add the times of all three parts.

steps.explain: Find the fraction of the journey that is left.
This remaining \(\dfrac25\) is 40 km, so one fifth is 20 km and the whole journey is 5 fifths.
Part 1: \(\dfrac25\) of 100 km is 40 km at 50 km/h.
Part 2: \(\dfrac15\) of 100 km is 20 km at 40 km/h.
Part 3 took half an hour (30 minutes). Add the three times.
Change 108 minutes to hours and minutes: 60 minutes is 1 hour.

questions.stem: A man bought 10 crates of oranges for \(\$80\) total. If he lost 2 of the crates, at what price would he have to sell each of the remaining crates in order to earn a total profit of 25 percent of the total cost?
questions.hint: Find the total money he needs to collect: the cost PLUS 25% profit on the cost. He can only sell the crates that are left, so share that money among the remaining crates.

keyPoints.note: Only 10 − 2 = 8 crates can be sold.

keyPoints.text: a total profit of 25 percent of the total cost
keyPoints.note: Total income = cost + 25% of cost = 125% of \(\$80\).

steps.explain: The crates that can be sold.
Total income needed: the cost plus a 25% profit, which is 125% of the cost.
Share the \(\$100\) among the 8 crates.
Check: \(8\times12.50=\$100\), and \(\$100\) is \(\$20\) more than the cost of \(\$80\), which is a profit of \(\dfrac{20}{80}=25\%\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: 100 students took part in a quiz. Their average score was 64 marks. The average score for the boys was 70 marks. The average score for the girls was 60 marks. How many more girls than boys took part in the competition?
questions.hint: Compare each group's average with the overall average of 64: boys are 6 above and girls are 4 below. The total “above” must cancel the total “below”. Or use the totals: total marks \(=\) 100 \(\times\) 64.

keyPoints.note: Total marks of all students = 100 × 64.

keyPoints.text: How many more girls than boys
keyPoints.note: Answer = girls − boys, not the number of girls.

steps.explain: Boys averaged 70, which is 6 more than the overall average of 64. Girls averaged 60, which is 4 less than 64.
The extra marks above 64 given by the boys must cancel the shortfall below 64 from the girls. Let there be \(b\) boys and \(g\) girls.
So \(b:g=4:6=2:3\). The total is 100 students, which is 5 parts, so each part is 20 students.
How many more girls than boys?
Check the total marks: \(40\times70+60\times60=2800+3600=6400=100\times64\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: At garage A, it costs \(\$8.75\) to park a car for the first hour and \(\$1.25\) for each additional hour. At garage B, it costs \(\$5.50\) for the first hour and \(\$2.50\) for each additional hour. What is the difference between the cost of parking a car for 5 hours at garage A and garage B?
questions.hint: For 5 hours there is 1 first hour and 4 ADDITIONAL hours. Work out the cost at each garage, then subtract.

keyPoints.note: The first hour is charged at a different price. The other 4 hours are the 'additional' hours.
Subtract the smaller cost from the larger cost.

steps.explain: 5 hours is the first hour plus 4 additional hours. Cost at garage A.
Cost at garage B.
Find the difference between the two costs.
Check: garage B is \(\$3.25\) cheaper for the first hour but \(\$1.25\) dearer for each of the 4 other hours. \(4\times1.25=5.00\), and \(5.00-3.25=1.75\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A pile of newspapers in Ms. McGrath's art class was \(17\dfrac34\) centimetres high. Each consecutive week, for the next 5 weeks, the height of the pile of newspapers increased by \(8\dfrac{7}{12}\) centimetres. What was the height, in centimetres, of the pile after 3 weeks?
questions.hint: After 3 weeks the pile has grown THREE times (not 5 times). Find the total growth in 3 weeks, then add it to the starting height. Use a common denominator of 12 for the fractions.

keyPoints.note: Use 3 weeks of growth, not the whole 5 weeks.
Each week the height goes up by the same amount: multiply by 3.

steps.explain: Growth in 3 weeks: \(3\times8\dfrac{7}{12}\). Multiply the whole number and the fraction separately.
Add: \(24+1\dfrac34=25\dfrac34\) cm of growth.
Add the growth to the starting height of \(17\dfrac34\).
Simplify \(\dfrac64=1\dfrac12\).
Check with decimals: \(17.75+3\times8.5833\ldots=17.75+25.75=43.5\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A student goes to school in the morning at 08:00 AM. He comes back when the smaller hand of the clock completes 180 degrees and the longer hand is at 12. What is the time when the student returns?
questions.hint: The smaller hand is the HOUR hand. It turns \(360^\circ\) in 12 hours, so it turns \(30^\circ\) every hour. Find how many hours are needed for \(180^\circ\), then add them to 8:00 am. The long (minute) hand at 12 means the time is exactly on the hour.

keyPoints.text: smaller hand of the clock completes 180 degrees
keyPoints.note: The hour hand is the smaller hand. It turns 30° per hour.
The minute hand is at 12, so the time is exactly on the hour.

steps.explain: The hour hand turns a full \(360^\circ\) in 12 hours, so in one hour it turns:
Find how many hours it takes to turn \(180^\circ\).
Add 6 hours to 08:00 AM.
The student returns at 2:00 pm (the minute hand is at 12, so it is exactly 2:00).
Check: half a turn of the hour hand is half of 12 hours = 6 hours. \(\checkmark\) The options 3:00 pm and 3.15 pm come from \(30^\circ\) per hour mistakes.

questions.hint: Use the labels on the picture: the front face is length \(l\) times height \(h\), the top face is \(l\) times \(w\), the side face is \(w\) times \(h\). Look for three whole numbers \(l\), \(w\), \(h\) whose pairs multiply to 15, 20 and 12.

keyPoints.text: What is the width, \(w\), of the box?
keyPoints.note: w is the receding edge, so it belongs to the top face (20) and the side face (12).

keyPoints.text: One face of a rectangular box has an area of 15 square centimetres
keyPoints.note: Face areas are products of two edges: l×h = 15, l×w = 20, w×h = 12.

steps.explain: Match each face with its two edges using the picture. Front face: \(l\times h=15\). Top face: \(l\times w=20\). Side face: \(w\times h=12\).

steps.explain: Look for factors. \(l\times h=15\) can be \(5\times3\) (or \(15\times1\)). Try \(l=5\) and \(h=3\).

Check the side face: \(w\times h=4\times3=12\). This matches.

keyPoints.note: Find the position of 24 in the whole list (counting left to right, then row by row).

steps.explain: Look at row I: 200, 192, 184, 176, 168, 160. Each number is 8 less than the one before. Row II starts with \(152=160-8\), so the pattern carries on from the end of one row to the start of the next.

steps.explain: The \(n\)th number in the list is \(200-8\times(n-1)\). For 24: \(200-8(n-1)=24\Rightarrow8(n-1)=176\Rightarrow n-1=22\).
Each row has 6 numbers. Rows I, II and III hold the first \(3\times6=18\) numbers. The 23rd number is the \(23-18=5\)th number in row IV.
The 5th column is column E.

steps.explain: Use the same pattern as the table: each number is 8 less than the one before it, so the \(n\)th number is \(200-8(n-1)\).

steps.explain: Find which position holds 8.
So 8 is the 25th number in the list.
Each row holds 6 numbers, so rows I to IV hold \(4\times6=24\) numbers. The 25th number is the FIRST number of row V, which is in column A.
Check: the last number of row IV (column F) is 16, and \(16-8=8\) starts row V. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Fourteen more than half the square of a certain number is 32. What is the number?
questions.hint: Translate the words into an equation, step by step. “The square of a number” is \(n^2\). “Half of it” is \(\frac12n^2\). “Fourteen more than” means add 14. Then undo the steps backwards.

keyPoints.text: Fourteen more than half the square of a certain number
keyPoints.note: Order of the words: square the number, take half, then add 14.

steps.explain: Write the words as an equation with \(n\) for the number.
Subtract 14 from both sides.
Multiply both sides by 2.
Find the positive number that multiplies by itself to give 36.
Check: the square of 6 is 36, half of it is 18, and 14 more is 32. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Terry writes a total of forty nine words on six blank cards. He writes eight words on each of the first five cards. How many words does Terry write on the last card?
questions.hint: Find how many words are on the first five cards altogether, then take that away from the total of 49.

keyPoints.text: eight words on each of the first five cards
keyPoints.note: 5 cards with 8 words each: multiply 5 × 8.
The last card has the words that are left over.

steps.explain: Find how many words are on the first five cards.
The total is 49 words, so the last card has the rest.
Check: \(5\times8+9=49\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Gary sells an article to Daniel at a profit of 25%. Daniel sells the same article to Dolly at a profit of 25%. If Dolly pays \(\$112.50\) for the article, for what price did Gary buy it?
questions.hint: Work backwards. A profit of 25% means the selling price is 125% (\(\dfrac54\)) of the cost. Dolly's price \(\$112.50\) is 125% of Daniel's cost. Do it twice.

keyPoints.note: Selling price = 125% of the buying price, so buying price = selling price ÷ 1.25.

keyPoints.text: for what price did Gary buy it
keyPoints.note: Go back two steps: Dolly's price → Daniel's cost → Gary's cost.

steps.explain: Dolly pays \(\$112.50\), which is 125% of what Daniel paid (Daniel made a 25% profit). Find Daniel's cost.
Daniel's cost of \(\$90\) is what Gary charged, which is 125% of what Gary paid (Gary made a 25% profit). Find Gary's cost.
Check forwards: Gary buys at \(\$72\) and sells at \(72\times1.25=\$90\). Daniel buys at \(\$90\) and sells at \(90\times1.25=\$112.50\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: If I fold a piece of square paper vertically, the new rectangle has an area of \(72\text{ cm}^2\). What is the perimeter of the original square?
questions.hint: Folding a square in half (vertically) makes a rectangle that is half the size of the square. Work out the area of the whole square first, then its side, then its perimeter (4 sides).

keyPoints.text: fold a piece of square paper vertically
keyPoints.note: A fold in half cuts the area in half: the rectangle is half of the square.
Perimeter = 4 × side. Do not use the rectangle's perimeter.

steps.explain: The folded rectangle is half of the square, so the square is double the area of the rectangle.
Find the side of the square: the number that multiplies by itself to give 144.
Perimeter of the square.
Check: the folded rectangle is 12 cm by 6 cm, with area \(12\times6=72\text{ cm}^2\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Shilla is counting aloud backwards from 99 in sixes, saying 99, 93, ... and so on. What is the last positive number she says?
questions.hint: Every number she says is 99 minus a multiple of 6. Divide 99 by 6 and look at the remainder: that is the smallest positive number she can reach.

keyPoints.note: She subtracts 6 each time: 99, 93, 87, ...
Stop just before the numbers go to 0 or below.

steps.explain: She takes away 6 each time, so the numbers she says are \(99-6\times k\). Divide 99 by 6 to find how many 6s can be taken away.
After taking away 6 sixteen times, she has taken away 96. What is left is the remainder.
The next number would be \(3-6=-3\), which is not positive. So 3 is the last positive number.
Check: the list ends 15, 9, 3 (all are 3 more than a multiple of 6). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: When 44 is added to a secret number, the result is three times more than the number. Find the secret number.
questions.hint: Let the secret number be \(n\). Adding 44 gives the same result as multiplying the number by 3. So \(n+44\) equals \(3\times n\). Solve this equation.

keyPoints.text: the result is three times more than the number
keyPoints.note: Read as: the result equals 3 times the number: n + 44 = 3n.

steps.explain: Let the secret number be \(n\). When 44 is added the result is 3 times the number.
Subtract \(n\) from both sides.
Divide both sides by 2.
Check: \(22+44=66\) and \(3\times22=66\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A plane left airport A at 8:30 pm on Tuesday and landed at airport B at 9:00 pm local time on the same day. If airport B is 19 hours behind airport A, how long did the trip take?
questions.hint: Compare the clocks at the SAME moment. When it is 8:30 pm at airport A, what time is it at airport B (19 hours behind)? Then find how long from that time until 9:00 pm at B.

keyPoints.text: airport B is 19 hours behind airport A
keyPoints.note: Airport B's clock shows a time that is 19 hours EARLIER than airport A's clock.

keyPoints.text: 9:00 pm local time on the same day
keyPoints.note: The landing time is on B's own clock.

steps.explain: When the plane takes off at 8:30 pm Tuesday at airport A, the clock at airport B is 19 hours behind. Take 19 hours off.
(From 8:30 pm go back 12 hours to 8:30 am, then 7 more hours to 1:30 am, on the same Tuesday.)
steps.work: \(8:30\text{ pm}-12\text{ h}=8:30\text{ am},\quad8:30\text{ am}-7\text{ h}=1:30\text{ am}\)

steps.explain: The plane lands at 9:00 pm Tuesday by the clock at B. Find the time from 1:30 am to 9:00 pm on B's clock: from 1:30 am to 1:30 pm is 12 hours, then to 9:00 pm is 7 hours 30 minutes.
So the trip took 19 hours 30 minutes.
Check: take off 8:30 pm at A. Add 19 h 30 min: 8:30 pm \(+\) 19 h \(=\) 3:30 pm next day, \(+\) 30 min \(=\) 4:00 pm Wednesday at A. At B (19 hours behind) it is 9:00 pm Tuesday. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The number 12\(\square\)6 is divisible by 3. What could not be the number in the box?
questions.hint: A number is divisible by 3 when the sum of its digits is a multiple of 3. Add the digits you know (1, 2 and 6), then check which box digits make the total a multiple of 3.

keyPoints.note: Divisibility test for 3: the digit sum must be divisible by 3.

keyPoints.text: What could not be the number in the box
keyPoints.note: Four options; three work and ONE does not. Find the one that fails.

steps.explain: Add the known digits.
The total digit sum is \(9+\square\). It must be a multiple of 3. Since 9 is already a multiple of 3, the box digit must also be a multiple of 3: 0, 3, 6 or 9.
Test the options: 0, 3 and 9 are multiples of 3 so they work (for example \(1206\), \(1236\), \(1296\)).
Test 8: \(1+2+8+6=17\), which is not a multiple of 3 (\(1286\div3=428.67\)). So 8 cannot go in the box.

questions.stem: What is the average of \(\dfrac12\) and \(\dfrac14\)?
questions.hint: The average of two numbers is their sum divided by 2. Add the fractions first using a common denominator, then divide by 2.

keyPoints.note: Average of two numbers = (first + second) ÷ 2.

steps.explain: Add the two fractions. Use the common denominator 4: \(\dfrac12=\dfrac24\).
Divide the sum by 2. Dividing by 2 is the same as multiplying by \(\dfrac12\).
Multiply the tops and the bottoms.
Check: \(\dfrac38\) lies between \(\dfrac14=\dfrac28\) and \(\dfrac12=\dfrac48\), exactly in the middle. \(\checkmark\) The option \(\dfrac34\) is the sum, not the average.

questions.stem: In a certain class, 3 out of 24 students are in student organizations. What is the ratio of students in student organizations to students not in student organizations?
questions.hint: The ratio compares the students IN organizations to the students NOT in organizations. Find the number not in organizations first (take away from 24), then write the ratio and simplify.

keyPoints.text: ratio of students in student organizations to students not in student organizations
keyPoints.note: It compares IN : NOT IN, not IN : all students.
3 students are in organizations, so 24 − 3 are not.

steps.explain: Find the number of students NOT in student organizations.
Write the ratio in the order asked: in organizations to not in organizations.
Simplify by dividing both numbers by 3.
As a fraction, 1 : 7 is written \(\dfrac17\).
Check the trap: \(\dfrac18=\dfrac{3}{24}\) compares the 3 students with ALL 24 students, not with the 21 who are not in organizations. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: The price of a newspaper rises from 5 cents to 15 cents. What is the percent increase in price?
questions.hint: Percent increase \(=\dfrac{\text{increase}}{\text{ORIGINAL price}}\times100\%\). Find the increase in cents first, then compare it with the ORIGINAL price (5 cents).

keyPoints.note: Compare the increase with the ORIGINAL price (5 cents), not the new price.
The increase is the new price minus the old price.

steps.explain: Find the increase in price.
Percent increase \(=\dfrac{\text{increase}}{\text{original}}\times100\%\).
Check: a 200% increase means adding 2 more times the original price: \(5+2\times5=15\). \(\checkmark\) The new price is 300% of the original, but the INCREASE is 200%.

questions.stem: What is the smallest integer greater than 1 that leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by any of the integers 6, 8, and 10?
questions.hint: If a number leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 6, 8 and 10, then the number MINUS 1 divides exactly by 6, 8 and 10. So find the lowest common multiple (LCM) of 6, 8 and 10 and add 1.

keyPoints.note: The number is 1 more than a common multiple of 6, 8 and 10.
Use the LOWEST common multiple, then add 1.

steps.explain: Find the lowest common multiple of 6, 8 and 10. Write prime factors: \(6=2\times3\), \(8=2^3\), \(10=2\times5\). Take the highest power of each prime.
A number that leaves remainder 1 is the common multiple plus 1.
Check: \(121=6\times20+1\), \(121=8\times15+1\), \(121=10\times12+1\). \(\checkmark\) The option 120 leaves remainder 0, and 21 and 41 do not work for all three numbers.

questions.stem:
Pat makes a sequence of numbers. He chooses a starting number and then subtracts equal amounts each time. The third number in his sequence is 45 and the tenth number is \(-32\).

What is the sixth number in the sequence?

questions.hint: Find the amount subtracted each time. From the 3rd number to the 10th number there are 7 steps. Then count 3 steps from the 3rd number to reach the 6th number.

keyPoints.note: The same amount is taken away at every step (a constant difference).

keyPoints.text: The third number in his sequence is 45 and the tenth number
keyPoints.note: Between the 3rd and the 10th number there are 10 − 3 = 7 steps.

steps.explain: Find the total drop from the 3rd number to the 10th number. Going from 45 down to \(-32\) crosses zero.

steps.explain: This drop of 77 happens over \(10-3=7\) equal steps, so find the amount subtracted each time.
The 6th number is 3 steps after the 3rd number (the 4th, 5th, 6th), so subtract \(3\times11\) from 45.

keyPoints.note: Identical trapeziums have equal areas, so divide the total by the number of trapeziums.
The trapeziums are the ring around the small square: big square − small square.

steps.explain: Area of the big square (side 12) and the small square (side 6).

Check with the trapezium formula: parallel sides 6 (half of the big side) and 3 (half of the small side), height 3. \(\dfrac{6+3}{2}\times3=4.5\times3=13.5\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Doris spent \(\dfrac23\) of her savings on a used car, and \(\dfrac14\) of her remainder on a new carpet. If the carpet cost her \(\$250\), how much were Doris' original savings?
questions.hint: Work backwards. The carpet cost \(\dfrac14\) of the REMAINDER (after the car), so find the remainder first. The remainder is also \(\dfrac13\) of her savings.

keyPoints.text: \(\dfrac14\) of her remainder on a new carpet
keyPoints.note: The carpet is a quarter of what was LEFT after buying the car, not a quarter of her savings.
Savings are the whole (100%). The remainder after the car is one third of the savings.

steps.explain: The carpet cost \(\$250\), which is one quarter of the remainder after the car. So the remainder is 4 times as much.
After spending \(\dfrac23\) on the car, she had \(\dfrac13\) of her savings left.
The whole savings is 3 times the remainder.
Check forwards: car \(=\dfrac23\times3000=\$2000\); left \(\$1000\); carpet \(=\dfrac14\times1000=\$250\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: At the Frosty Ice Cream store, the number of cones sold fell by 20 percent in November. If sales fell by a further 25 percent in December, what was the percent decrease in the number of cones sold in the whole two-month period?
questions.hint: Do not just add 20% and 25%. The second fall is 25% of the NEW (smaller) number. Pick a starting number such as 100 cones and follow it through the two months.

keyPoints.note: After a 20% fall, 80% of the original number is left.
25% of the November number, not of the original number.

steps.explain: Start with 100 cones in October. A 20% fall in November leaves 80%.
In December the sales fall by 25% of the November amount (80 cones), leaving 75% of 80.
Compare the final amount with the original amount.
So the percent decrease over the two months is:
Check with multipliers: \(0.8\times0.75=0.6\), which is 60% left, so a 40% decrease. The option 45% comes from wrongly adding \(20\%+25\%\). \(\checkmark\)

meta.source: Mastering Mathematics Book 1 · Selective and Scholarship Tests

questions.stem: Twenty four more than half of a number is 49. What is the number?
questions.hint: Work backwards from 49. Undo the “add 24” first, then undo the “half” by doubling.

keyPoints.text: Twenty four more than half of a number
keyPoints.note: Order: take half of the number, then add 24.

steps.explain: Let the number be \(n\). Half of it, plus 24, is 49.
Subtract 24 from both sides to undo the adding.
Multiply both sides by 2 to undo the halving.
Check: half of 50 is 25, and 24 more than 25 is 49. \(\checkmark\) The option 25 is the HALF of the number, not the number.

questions.stem: A car travels at \(\dfrac23\) the speed of a motor bike. If it takes the motor bike 2 hours to travel 200 km, how many hours will the trip take the car?
questions.hint: The car is SLOWER than the bike, so it takes LONGER for the same trip. Find the bike's speed, then the car's speed (two thirds of the bike's), then time \(=\) distance \(\div\) speed.

keyPoints.text: \(\dfrac23\) the speed of a motor bike
keyPoints.note: The car goes at 2/3 of the bike's speed, so it needs 3/2 of the bike's time.

keyPoints.text: how many hours will the trip take the car
keyPoints.note: Use the same 200 km distance for the car.

steps.explain: Speed of the motor bike: distance \(\div\) time.
The car's speed is two thirds of the bike's speed.
Time for the car: distance \(\div\) speed.
Check with the shortcut: a car at \(\dfrac23\) the speed takes \(\dfrac32\) of the time: \(\dfrac32\times2=3\) hours. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Divide \(\$15.20\) among three people so that the second will have one dollar more than the first, and the third will have \(\$2.70\) more than the second. What is the greatest amount received?
questions.hint: Let the FIRST person get \(x\). Write the second and third amounts in terms of \(x\) (watch out: the third has \(\$2.70\) more than the SECOND, not the first). The three amounts must add to \(\$15.20\).

keyPoints.text: the third will have \(\$2.70\) more than the second

keyPoints.note: The answer is the amount of the third person.

steps.explain: Let the first person receive \(x\) dollars. The second has 1 more, and the third has 2.70 more than the second.
The three amounts add to \(\$15.20\).
Collect like terms: \(3x+4.70=15.20\). Subtract 4.70, then divide by 3.
Find the three amounts.
The greatest amount is the third person's.

questions.stem: An abundant number is a positive integer whose factors (other than the number itself) have a sum greater than the number. Which number is not abundant?
questions.hint: For each option, list all the factors EXCEPT the number itself, add them up, and compare the sum with the number. The number that is NOT abundant has a factor sum that is NOT greater than the number.

keyPoints.note: Include 1 but do NOT include the number itself.
Find the one where the sum of the other factors is not bigger than the number.

steps.explain: Test 18. Factors other than 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9.
Test 12. Factors other than 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6.
Test 24. Factors other than 24: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 12.
Test 16. Factors other than 16: 1, 2, 4, 8.
The sum 15 is less than 16, so 16 is not abundant.

questions.stem: One scoop of fish food can feed 7 fish for two days. How many fish can 6 scoops of fish food feed for a week?
questions.hint: First find how many fish the 6 scoops can feed for TWO days. A week is longer than two days, so the same food can feed FEWER fish for a week. Find how many times longer a week is than 2 days.

keyPoints.note: 1 scoop feeds 7 fish for 2 days.
A week is 7 days, which is 3.5 times as long as 2 days.

steps.explain: 6 scoops feed 6 times as many fish as one scoop for two days.
A week (7 days) is longer than 2 days. How many times longer?
The same food lasts 3.5 times longer if there are 3.5 times FEWER fish, so divide by 3.5.
Check with fish-days: 6 scoops give \(42\times2=84\) fish-days of food. For 7 days the number of fish is \(84\div7=12\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A dozen balls cost you \(\$40\). You get every fifth ball for free. How many balls do you get for \(\$100\)?
questions.hint: Find the price of ONE ball you actually pay for. In 12 balls, the 5th and the 10th are free, so you pay for only 10 of them. Then find how many balls you pay for with \(\$100\), and add the free ones (1 free ball for every 4 paid).

keyPoints.note: A dozen is 12 balls, and 2 of them are free, so the \(\$40\) pays for 10 balls.
For every 4 balls you pay for, you get a 5th one free.

steps.explain: In a dozen balls the 5th and 10th balls are free, so you pay for 10 balls.
The price of one paid ball.
With \(\$100\) you can pay for:
For every 4 paid balls you get 1 free ball, so with 25 paid balls the free balls are:
Add the paid and free balls.
Check: 31 balls have free balls at positions 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, which is 6 free balls, so \(31-6=25\) paid balls costing \(25\times\$4=\$100\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Americans measure the temperature in \(^\circ\text{F}\). Australians measure the temperature in \(^\circ\text{C}\). The formula to convert Fahrenheit to Celsius is \(C=\dfrac{5\times(F-32)}{9}\) where F represents the temperature in \(^\circ\text{F}\) and C represents the temperature in \(^\circ\text{C}\). What is the temperature in \(^\circ\text{F}\) when it is \(20^\circ\text{C}\)?
questions.hint: Put \(C=20\) into the formula and solve for \(F\). Undo the operations in reverse order: multiply by 9, divide by 5, then add 32.

keyPoints.note: Replace C with 20 and solve for F step by step.

steps.explain: Substitute \(C=20\) into the formula.
Multiply both sides by 9 to remove the fraction.
Divide both sides by 5.
Add 32 to both sides.
Check: \(F=68\) gives \(C=\dfrac{5\times(68-32)}{9}=\dfrac{5\times36}{9}=\dfrac{180}{9}=20\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Four sisters are all 3 years apart in age. The total of their ages is equal to 26 years. How old is the eldest sister?
questions.hint: The sisters' ages are the youngest's age, then 3 more, 6 more, and 9 more. Add the extra years first, take them away from 26, and share the rest equally between the four sisters.

keyPoints.note: Each sister is 3 years older than the next younger one: +0, +3, +6, +9.

keyPoints.text: How old is the eldest sister
keyPoints.note: The eldest is the youngest's age plus 9.

steps.explain: Let the youngest be \(x\) years old. The ages are \(x\), \(x+3\), \(x+6\) and \(x+9\).
The ages add up to 26.
Subtract 18, then divide by 4.
The eldest sister is 9 years older than the youngest.
Check: the ages are 2, 5, 8, 11 and \(2+5+8+11=26\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Alannah needs six tacks to fix two rectangular pictures because she can overlap the pictures. What is the number of tacks she needs to tack 120 pictures if she continues to hang the pictures horizontally?

questions.hint: Find a pattern. The first picture needs 4 tacks (one in each corner). Each new overlapping picture shares its left edge with the picture before it, so it only needs 2 NEW tacks. Look for a formula (tacks \(=\) 2 \(\times\) number of pictures + something).

keyPoints.text: six tacks to fix two rectangular pictures
keyPoints.note: The overlap lets two pictures share 2 tacks: 2 pictures need 6 tacks, not 8.
Use the pattern to find the number of tacks for 120 pictures.

steps.explain: For 1 picture 4 tacks are needed (the four corners). For 2 overlapping pictures 6 tacks are needed (the red dots). Each extra picture adds only the 2 tacks on its far edge, because its near edge shares the tacks of the previous picture.

questions.stem: Simone cut a cake into two halves and then one half into smaller pieces of equal size. Each of the small pieces is one hundred and twenty grams in weight. If she has eight pieces of the cake altogether, how heavy was the original cake?
questions.hint: Count carefully: she has 8 pieces ALTOGETHER. One of the pieces is the uncut half; the other pieces are the small ones. Find the weight of the half cake, then double it.

keyPoints.note: Only ONE half was cut into small pieces. The other half is still one big piece.

keyPoints.text: eight pieces of the cake altogether
keyPoints.note: 8 pieces = 1 uncut half + 7 small pieces.

steps.explain: She has 8 pieces altogether. One piece is the uncut half, so the cut half is made of the other pieces.
Each small piece weighs 120 g, so the cut half weighs:
The other half is the same weight, so the whole cake is double.

Check: the uncut half is 840 g, the 7 small pieces make 840 g, and \(840+840=1680\). The option 960 would come from 8 pieces of 120 g, which wrongly treats the uncut half as a small piece. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: When a number is divided by half and the result is subtracted 44 the answer is 44. What is the number?
questions.hint: “Divided by half” means \(\div\dfrac12\), which makes the number TWICE as big. Write an equation and undo the steps in reverse order.

keyPoints.note: Dividing by one half is the same as multiplying by 2 (how many halves fit into the number).
After dividing, take away 44 and the result is 44.

steps.explain: Let the number be \(n\). Dividing by \(\dfrac12\) gives \(n\div\dfrac12=2n\). Then 44 is subtracted and the answer is 44.
Add 44 to both sides.
Divide both sides by 2.
Check: \(44\div\dfrac12=88\), and \(88-44=44\). \(\checkmark\) The option 88 is \(2n\), the number AFTER dividing by half.

questions.stem: Peter took 2 Maths tests. There were 40 questions in Test 1. In Test 2 Peter got 23 correct and 7 incorrect. When the results from both tests were added together Peter got 18 more questions correct than incorrect. How many questions did Peter get correct in Test 1?
questions.hint: Find the total number of questions in both tests, then use “correct \(-\) incorrect \(=\) 18” together with “correct \(+\) incorrect \(=\) total” to find the TOTAL correct. Then take away the correct answers from Test 2.

keyPoints.note: Test 2 has 23 + 7 = 30 questions.
Total correct − total incorrect = 18, for both tests together.

steps.explain: Total number of questions in both tests: Test 1 has 40 and Test 2 has \(23+7=30\).
Let \(C\) be the total correct and \(I\) the total incorrect. Then \(C+I=70\) and \(C-I=18\). Add the two equations.
So 44 questions were correct altogether. Test 2 had 23 correct, so Test 1 had the rest.
Check: Test 1 has 21 correct and 19 incorrect. Totals: correct \(21+23=44\), incorrect \(19+7=26\), and \(44-26=18\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: A rectangular container, 15 cm long, 10 cm wide and 12 cm high, holds water to a depth of 4 cm. When a stone of volume \(300\text{ cm}^3\) is placed in the water, the water level rises. What is the new height of the water level?
questions.hint: The stone pushes up the water level. The volume of water it pushes aside equals the volume of the stone. Find how far a volume of 300 cm\(^3\) raises the level over the base of the container (15 cm by 10 cm). Remember to ADD this rise to the 4 cm already there.

keyPoints.note: The water rises by a volume equal to the stone: 300 cm³ spread over the base.
New height = old depth (4 cm) + rise.

steps.explain: The base of the container is 15 cm by 10 cm. Find its area.
The stone raises the water over the whole base. Rise \(=\) volume \(\div\) base area.
The water was 4 cm deep, so the new depth is 2 cm more.
Check: the container is 12 cm high, so 6 cm is allowed. New volume of water plus stone \(=150\times4+300=900\), and \(150\times6=900\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.hint: Look at the LAST digits of the powers: 3, 9, 7, 1, 3, 9, ... They repeat in a cycle. Find the length of the cycle and use the remainder when 2003 is divided by it.

keyPoints.note: You do not need to calculate the number: only its last digit, using the repeating pattern.

steps.explain: List the last digits of the powers of 3: \(3^1\to3\), \(3^2\to9\), \(3^3\to7\), \(3^4\to1\), \(3^5\to3\), \(3^6\to9\), ... The pattern 3, 9, 7, 1 repeats every 4 powers.
Divide the power 2003 by the length of the cycle, 4, and look at the remainder.
The remainder 3 means the last digit is the 3rd one in the cycle 3, 9, 7, 1, which is 7.
Check with smaller powers: \(3^3=27\) ends in 7 and 3 is the remainder of \(3\div4\); \(3^7=2187\) also ends in 7 (and 7 has remainder 3 when divided by 4). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: What is the smallest integer that can be written entirely with zeros and ones and is evenly divisible by 15?
questions.hint: \(15=3\times5\), so the number must be divisible by BOTH 3 and 5. A number divisible by 5 ends in 0 or 5; since only 0 and 1 may be used, it must end in 0. A number divisible by 3 has a digit sum that is a multiple of 3.

keyPoints.note: Divisible by 15 means divisible by 3 and by 5 at the same time.

keyPoints.text: written entirely with zeros and ones
keyPoints.note: Only the digits 0 and 1 can appear, so the digit sum is just the number of 1s.

steps.explain: A number divisible by 5 must end in 0 or 5. With only the digits 0 and 1 allowed, the last digit must be 0.
A number divisible by 3 has a digit sum that is a multiple of 3. With only 0s and 1s, the digit sum is the number of 1s, so there must be 3 (or 6, ...) ones.
Check the options for these two rules. Option A, 11110, has four 1s (digit sum 4). Option B, 10011, and option C, 11101, end in 1. Option D, 10110, ends in 0 and has three 1s.
Test by dividing: \(10110\div15=674\), so option D is divisible by 15.
So among the choices, only 10110 is divisible by 15. (A smaller number such as 1110 also works, but it is not one of the choices.)

questions.stem: James and Angela have the same amount of money. How much must James give to Angela so that she has forty more than he?
questions.hint: When James gives some money to Angela, James LOSES that amount and Angela GAINS the same amount, so the gap between them changes by TWICE the amount given. They start with a gap of 0.

keyPoints.note: They start equal: the difference is 0.

keyPoints.text: she has forty more than he
keyPoints.note: The final difference is 40, which is made of the gift counted twice.

steps.explain: Let James give \(x\) dollars. James has \(x\) dollars less and Angela has \(x\) dollars more than before. Since they started equal, the difference at the end is:
This difference must be 40 dollars.
Divide both sides by 2.
Check with an example: each starts with \(\$100\). James gives \(\$20\): James \(\$80\), Angela \(\$120\). The difference is \(\$40\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.hint: On a balance, the side that hangs LOWER is the HEAVIER side. Compare the two ends of each bar. First compare A and B (left bar), then C and B (right bar), then compare the left half with the right half of the top bar.

steps.explain: Left bar (A and B): the bar is lower on the B side, so B is heavier than A.

Top bar: the right side (C + B) hangs lower than the left side (A + B), so C + B is heavier than A + B. B is on both sides, so C must be heavier than A.

Put the facts together: \(B\gt C\gt A\). So B is the heaviest and C is heavier than A. Check each statement: A (same weight) is false; B (A is heavier than C) is false; C (A + B is not lighter than B + C) is false because A + B is lighter; D (C is heavier than A and B is the heaviest) is true.

questions.stem: There are 30 students in a class. 22 students have red stars, 8 students have green crosses and 6 students have nothing. How many students have both?
questions.hint: First find how many students have at least one item (30 minus those with nothing). If you add 22 and 8 you count the students who have BOTH items twice. Compare the two totals.

keyPoints.note: These 6 have no star and no cross, so 30 − 6 have at least one item.
Students counted twice when adding 22 + 8 are the ones who have both.

steps.explain: Students who have at least one item (a star, a cross, or both).
If we add the red-star students and the green-cross students, those with BOTH are counted twice.
The count 30 is more than the real number 24 by exactly the number of students counted twice.
Check: 6 have both, \(22-6=16\) have only a star, \(8-6=2\) have only a cross, and 6 have nothing. \(6+16+2+6=30\). \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Dan has 99 eggs to pack into boxes. Each box can hold a dozen eggs. How many boxes will Dan need?
questions.hint: A dozen is 12. Divide 99 by 12. If there are eggs left over, they still need a box, so round UP.

keyPoints.note: A dozen means 12.

keyPoints.text: How many boxes will Dan need
keyPoints.note: Boxes are whole: leftover eggs still need one more box.

steps.explain: Divide the eggs by 12 eggs per box.
8 boxes hold \(8\times12=96\) eggs, so 3 eggs are left over. They need another box.
So Dan needs one more box than 8.
Check: 9 boxes hold up to \(9\times12=108\) eggs, which is enough for 99. \(\checkmark\)

questions.stem: Ten marbles are distributed among Alana, Ben, Cathy and David such that everybody gets at least two, and each girl gets one marble more than David. How many marbles do the girls get in total?
questions.hint: Alana and Cathy are the girls; Ben and David are the boys. David has at least 2 marbles and each girl has 1 more than David. Try the smallest numbers and see what fits the total of 10.

keyPoints.text: each girl gets one marble more than David
keyPoints.note: Girls get David's number + 1 each.
Nobody has fewer than 2 marbles, so David has at least 2.

steps.explain: The girls are Alana and Cathy. Everybody gets at least 2, so David has at least 2. Try David \(=2\): each girl then gets \(2+1=3\). Ben must also have at least 2.
Add up with Ben \(=2\).
Check that David cannot have more: if David had 3, each girl would have 4, and \(3+4+4=11\) is already more than 10. So David \(=2\) and Ben \(=2\) is the only possibility.
The girls (Alana and Cathy) have 3 marbles each.

keyPoints.text: What fraction is the shaded area of the area of the triangle

questions.stem: How many revolutions does a wheel of circumference 2.1 metres make in travelling 4.2 kilometres?
questions.hint: Change kilometres to metres first so that both distances are in the same unit. In one revolution the wheel travels one circumference, so divide the total distance by the circumference.

keyPoints.note: Change to metres: 1 km = 1000 m.
One revolution covers a distance equal to the circumference.

steps.explain: Change the distance into metres.
One revolution covers 2.1 m, so the number of revolutions is the distance divided by the circumference.
Multiply the top and bottom by 10 to remove the decimal point: \(42\,000\div21\).
Check: \(2000\times2.1=4200\) m. \(\checkmark\) The option 2 is the answer if you forget to change km into metres.

questions.stem: On an international flight, you are allowed to take 20 kg of baggage. If you take more you must pay \(\$8.50\) per extra kilogram. How much did Angela's baggage weigh if she had to pay \(\$76.50\)?
questions.hint: She paid only for the EXTRA kilograms above 20 kg. Find how many extra kilograms \(\$76.50\) pays for, then add them to the 20 kg she was allowed.

keyPoints.text: allowed to take 20 kg of baggage
keyPoints.note: The first 20 kg are free. Only kilograms above 20 are charged.

keyPoints.text: How much did Angela's baggage weigh
keyPoints.note: Total weight = 20 kg allowed + the extra kilograms.

steps.explain: The payment of \(\$76.50\) is for the extra kilograms, at \(\$8.50\) each.
Add the extra weight to the free allowance of 20 kg.
Check: 9 extra kg cost \(9\times8.50=\$76.50\). \(\checkmark\) The option 9 kg is only the EXTRA weight.

keyPoints.text: straight line connecting P and Q on this circle

steps.explain: An arc is a curved part of the circle, not a straight line, so it is not an arc.

steps.explain: A radius goes from the centre O to a point on the circle. The line PQ does not touch O, so it is not a radius.
A diameter is a chord that passes through the centre O. The line PQ does not pass through O, so it is not a diameter.
A chord is any straight line joining two points on the circle. PQ joins P and Q, so it is a chord.
